rows.class_notes: Asymmetric strengthening of Conjecture 1.2 that implies Caccetta-Haggkvist; real parameters alpha,beta.

rows.title: Conjecture 1.4
rows.paper_title: Sparse graphs with no polynomial-sized anticomplete pairs
rows.statement_text: For every graph $H$ there exists $\varepsilon > 0$ such that in every $H$-free $\varepsilon$-bounded graph $G$ with $|G| > 1$ vertices, there is an anticomplete $(\varepsilon|G|, \varepsilon|G|)$-pair.
rows.context_text: A graph $G$ is $\varepsilon$-bounded if its maximum degree is less than $\varepsilon|G|$. By a theorem of Rödl, $H$ satisfies Conjecture 1.3 if and only if both $H$ and $\bar{H}$ satisfy Conjecture 1.4, so the two conjectures are equivalent over all $H$. For certain graphs $H$, however, 1.4 is more tractable than 1.3.
rows.source_text: For every graph $H$ there exists $\varepsilon > 0$ such that in every $H$-free $\varepsilon$-bounded graph $G$ with $|G| > 1$ vertices, there is an anticomplete $(\varepsilon|G|, \varepsilon|G|)$-pair.
rows.verification_note: Authored in X58.v:epsilon_bounded_h_free_anticomplete_pair_statement. Encodes Conjecture 1.4: epsilon-bounded H-free graphs contain a linear anticomplete pair.
rows.status_semantics: Conjecture 1.4 from arXiv:1810.00058 remains open in full generality. Partial progress has been made: Fox, Nguyen, Scott, and Seymour (arXiv:2307.00801) proved the conjecture for H=P4 with the optimal bound δ=ε, and more generally for all graphs H obtainable by vertex-substitution from copies of P4 and its subgraphs, via the stronger 'viral' property. Separately, Bucić, Fox, and Pham (arXiv:2403.08303) proved that the polynomial Rödl conjecture (Conjecture 1.3 in the source paper, which is equivalent to Conjecture 1.4 over all H by Rödl's theorem) is equivalent to the Erdős-Hajnal conjecture, establishing that the full resolution of Conjecture 1.4 is as hard as settling Erdős-Hajnal.
rows.class_notes: epsilon-bounded defined in context; anticomplete pair is standard vocabulary.

rows.title: Open Problem: 3-colourability of ternary graphs
rows.paper_title: Proof of the Kalai-Meshulam conjecture
rows.statement_text: It may be that all ternary graphs are 3-colourable.
rows.context_text: Bonamy, Charbit and Thomassé proved that every ternary graph is $c$-colourable for some absolute constant $c$, and a stronger result by two of the present authors shows bounded chromatic number whenever clique number is bounded and no induced cycle has length $p\bmod q$. The paper notes that whether the bound can be taken to be 3 for ternary graphs specifically remains open.
rows.source_text: It may be that all ternary graphs are 3-colourable.

rows.title: Conjecture 1.5 (sparse strong EH-property)
rows.paper_title: Caterpillars in Erdős-Hajnal
rows.statement_text: A graph $H$ has the sparse strong EH-property if and only if $H$ is a forest.
rows.context_text: The sparse strong EH-property of $H$ requires that there exists $\varepsilon > 0$ such that every $H$-free graph $G$ with $|V(G)| \geq 2$ either has a vertex with at least $\varepsilon|V(G)|$ neighbours or contains two anticomplete sets of vertices each of cardinality at least $\varepsilon|V(G)|$. Erdős's construction shows the property forces $H$ to be a forest; the conjecture asserts the converse.
rows.source_text: A graph $H$ has the sparse strong EH-property if and only if $H$ is a forest.
rows.verification_note: Authored in X57.v:sparse_strong_eh_iff_forest_statement. Encodes Conjecture 1.5: sparse strong EH-property iff H is a forest.
rows.status_semantics: Conjecture 1.5 is fully resolved. The 'only if' direction — that the sparse strong EH-property forces H to be a forest — was already known from Erdős's construction. The converse — that every forest H has the sparse strong EH-property — was proved by Chudnovsky, Scott, Seymour, and Spirkl in 'Pure Pairs. I. Trees and Linear Anticomplete Pairs' (arXiv:1809.00919), which appeared as an arXiv preprint in September 2018 (one month before the caterpillar paper) and was published in Advances in Mathematics in 2020; Seymour and Spirkl are co-authors on both papers.
rows.class_notes: Sparse strong EH-property fully defined in context; a sparse variant of Erdos-Hajnal, solved.

rows.title: Question 1.3
rows.paper_title: Colouring Graphs with Sparse Neighbourhoods: Bounds and Applications
rows.statement_text: Let $G$ be a $\lfloor (1-\varepsilon)(\Delta(G)+1) \rfloor + 1$-critical graph with $\omega(G) \leq (1-\alpha)(\Delta(G)+1)$. What is the largest $\delta = \delta(\varepsilon,\alpha)$, such that $G$ is $\delta$-sparse?
rows.context_text: This question isolates the first of two steps in the King–Reed proof strategy for Reed's conjecture: showing that a graph which is critical with respect to a list assignment and has bounded clique number must have sparse neighbourhoods. Improving $\delta$ directly strengthens the $\varepsilon$ achievable in Theorem 1.2.
rows.source_text: Let $G$ be a $\lfloor (1-\varepsilon)(\Delta(G)+1) \rfloor + 1$-critical graph with $\omega(G) \leq (1-\alpha)(\Delta(G)+1)$. What is the largest $\delta = \delta(\varepsilon,\alpha)$, such that $G$ is $\delta$-sparse?
rows.status_semantics: Question 1.3 asks for the optimal δ(ε,α) quantifying how sparse a critical graph with bounded clique number must be — Step 1 of the King–Reed strategy for Reed's conjecture. A 2020 master's thesis by Kroeker (supervised by Postle at UWaterloo) directly addresses sparsity of list-critical graphs with small clique number, deriving new density lemmas by embedding the graph in a complete multipartite graph with many parts of size three. Kelly and Postle (arXiv:1911.02672) separately prove an improved lower bound on the density of k-critical graphs with clique number less than k/2. Neither work fully determines the optimal δ(ε,α), so the question remains open.
rows.defer_reason: Asks for the largest function delta(eps,alpha), a determine-the-value question, and 'delta-sparse' is not defined in the record.

rows.title: Question 1.4
rows.paper_title: Colouring Graphs with Sparse Neighbourhoods: Bounds and Applications
rows.statement_text: Let $G$ be a $\delta$-sparse graph. What is the largest $\varepsilon = \varepsilon(\delta)$ such that $\chi(G) \leq (1-\varepsilon)(\Delta+1)$?
rows.context_text: This isolates the second step in the King–Reed proof: given neighbourhood sparsity, bound the chromatic number below $\Delta+1$. Molloy–Reed obtained $\varepsilon(\delta)\approx 0.0238\delta$ and Bruhn–Joos improved to $\approx 0.1827\delta - 0.0778\delta^{3/2}$; the paper further improves this using an iterative naive colouring procedure.
rows.source_text: Let $G$ be a $\delta$-sparse graph. What is the largest $\varepsilon = \varepsilon(\delta)$ such that $\chi(G) \leq (1-\varepsilon)(\Delta+1)$?
rows.status_semantics: The exact optimal function ε(δ) characterising the best chromatic bound for δ-sparse graphs remains unknown. Hurley, de Joannis de Verclos, and Kang (arXiv:2007.07874, Advances in Combinatorics 2022) directly improved the lower bound on ε(δ) via an iterated colouring procedure for graphs of bounded local density (the same σ-sparse setting), claiming their leading term is asymptotically optimal as σ→0 and surpassing the Bonamy–Perrett–Postle bound. No paper has determined the exact value of ε(δ) for any specific δ > 0.
rows.defer_reason: Asks for the largest function eps(delta); determine-the-optimal-constant question, not a single proposition.

rows.title: Conjecture 1.8
rows.paper_title: Additive Approximation of Generalized Turán Questions
rows.statement_text: For every graph $T$, family of graphs $\mathcal{F}$ such that no $F \in \mathcal{F}$ is a subgraph of a blow-up of $T$, and $\epsilon > 0$, it is NP-hard to approximate $\mathrm{ex}(G, T, \mathcal{F})$ up to additive error of $n^{v(T)-\epsilon}$ for a given input graph $G$ on $n$ vertices.
rows.context_text: The authors prove Theorem 1.7 as a special case (for $T = K_m$, $\mathcal{F} = \{K_k\}$ with $k \geq m+2$) and note that Proposition 1.5 covers the complementary easy regime (when some $F \in \mathcal{F}$ is a subgraph of a blow-up of $T$). They believe that excluding those easy cases no significantly better approximation than $\epsilon n^{v(T)}$ is achievable in polynomial time, leading to this conjecture. Section 6 of the paper contains further remarks on this conjecture and related open problems.
rows.source_text: For every graph $T$, family of graphs $\mathcal{F}$ such that no $F \in \mathcal{F}$ is a subgraph of a blow-up of $T$, and $\epsilon > 0$, it is NP-hard to approximate $\mathrm{ex}(G, T, \mathcal{F})$ up to additive error of $n^{v(T)-\epsilon}$ for a given input graph $G$ on $n$ vertices.
rows.class_notes: NP-hardness of additive approximation of generalized Turan numbers; precise once a hardness framework exists.

rows.title: Problem 2.15
rows.paper_title: On the Complexity of Digraph Colourings and Vertex Arboricity
rows.statement_text: Let $F$ be a fixed (multi-)digraph. Instance: A (multi-)digraph $D$. Decide whether $D$ is circularly $F$-colourable.
rows.context_text: A digraph $D$ is circularly $F$-colourable if there exists a circular homomorphism from $D$ to $F$. This problem generalises Problem 1 and serves as a directed analogue of the $H$-colouring problem for graphs. Conjecture 2.16 asserts that NP-completeness holds whenever $F$ contains a directed cycle, and Theorem 2.17 establishes this for almost all such cases.
rows.source_text: Let $F$ be a fixed (multi-)digraph. Instance: A (multi-)digraph $D$. Decide whether $D$ is circularly $F$-colourable.
rows.status_semantics: Problem 2.15 asks for the complexity of deciding circular F-colourability for a fixed digraph F. Conjecture 2.16 (stated in the same paper) asserts this problem is NP-complete whenever F contains a directed cycle. Theorem 2.17 of the source paper already establishes NP-completeness for almost all such F: specifically for digon-free digraphs with directed cycles, digraphs whose symmetric part contains an odd cycle, and 2-colourable digraphs. The remaining open case is digraphs F that contain a directed cycle whose symmetric part is non-empty and bipartite. No external follow-up paper resolving the full conjecture was found in the literature.

The sole remaining open case is F containing a directed cycle whose symmetric part is non-empty, bipartite, and such that F is not 2-colourable; no subsequent work resolving this case was found in the literature.

rows.title: Problem 5.40
rows.paper_title: On the Complexity of Digraph Colourings and Vertex Arboricity
rows.statement_text: For given $k,b\in\mathbb{N}$ with $k\geq b$, is there a directed graph $\vec{K}(k,b)$ with vertex set $\binom{[k]}{b}$ such that the following holds? The subdigraph of $\vec{K}(k,b)$ induced by any $\{B_{1},\ldots,B_{l}\}\subseteq\binom{[k]}{b}$ is acylic if and only if $\bigcap_{i=1}^{l}{B_{i}}\neq\emptyset$.
rows.context_text: Such 'directed Kneser graphs' $\vec{K}(k,b)$ would allow $b$-tuple $k$-colourings of digraphs to be equivalent to the existence of circular homomorphisms to $\vec{K}(k,b)$, tying the fractional dichromatic number to circular homomorphism theory. Existence is confirmed for $k=b+1$ via the directed cycle of length $b+1$, but the general case is open.

rows.title: Problem 4
rows.paper_title: 1-subdivisions, fractional chromatic number and Hall ratio
rows.statement_text: Determine the smallest function $g : \mathbb{Z}^+ \to \mathbb{R}^+$ such that for every graph $G$, $\chi_f(G) \leq \rho(G)\,g(|V(G)|)$.
rows.context_text: Since $\chi_f(G) = O(\rho(G) \log n)$ follows from a greedy independent-set argument, and the graphs produced by Corollary 3 have doubly exponential size in their fractional chromatic number (giving $g(n) = \Omega(\log\log n)$), the true growth rate of the smallest such $g$ is unknown.
rows.source_text: Determine the smallest function $g : \mathbb{Z}^+ \to \mathbb{R}^+$ such that for every graph $G$, $\chi_f(G) \leq \rho(G)\,g(|V(G)|)$.
rows.status_semantics: Problem 4 asks for the exact growth rate of the smallest function $g$ such that $\chi_f(G) \leq \rho(G)\,g(|V(G)|)$ for all graphs $G$; at the time of posting the bounds were $\Omega(\log\log n) \leq g(n) \leq O(\log n)$. Steiner (2024, arXiv:2411.16465, published in Combinatorica) substantially narrows this gap by proving a lower bound of $\Omega(\log n/(\log\log n)^3)$, establishing $g(n) = (\log n)^{1-o(1)}$ and showing the growth rate is essentially logarithmic. The exact smallest $g$ (precise constant factors) remains undetermined, so the problem is partially resolved.

rows.title: Problem 5
rows.paper_title: 1-subdivisions, fractional chromatic number and Hall ratio
rows.statement_text: Do there exist, for some constant $c > 0$, graphs $G$ of arbitrarily large fractional chromatic number such that $\rho(G) \leq c$ and $\alpha_{\deg_H}(H) \geq |E(H)|/c$ for every $H \subseteq G$?
rows.context_text: To lower-bound $\chi_f$ of the probabilistically constructed graphs in Theorem 1, the authors assign vertex weights proportional to degrees. Problem 5 asks whether such degree-weighted independence certificates can simultaneously be large while the ordinary Hall ratio remains bounded, motivating a search for intermediate weight families $\mathcal{F}$ between $\{0,1\}$-valued weights (Hall ratio) and all non-negative weights (fractional chromatic number).
rows.source_text: Do there exist, for some constant $c > 0$, graphs $G$ of arbitrarily large fractional chromatic number such that $\rho(G) \leq c$ and $\alpha_{\deg_H}(H) \geq |E(H)|/c$ for every $H \subseteq G$?
rows.status_semantics: Problem 5 was affirmatively solved by Raphael Steiner (arXiv:2411.16465, published in Combinatorica 2025). Theorem 1.5 of that paper constructs, for every fixed δ > 0 and sufficiently large n, an n-vertex graph G with χ_f(G) ≥ log log n / (50 log log log n), ρ(G) ≤ 4 + δ, and α_{deg_H}(H) ≥ |E(H)| / (4 + δ) for every subgraph H ⊆ G, directly answering the problem in the affirmative. The companion arXiv:2007.11853 (Dvořák, on weighted sublinear separators) does not bear on Problem 5.
rows.class_notes: Yes/no existence question (solved), but the degree-weighted independence notation alpha_degH is not defined in the record.

rows.title: Problem 1.4
rows.paper_title: The hat guessing number of graphs
rows.statement_text: Do there exist functions $f_i : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, $1 \leq i \leq 3$ such that (i) if the maximum degree of $G$ is $\Delta$, then $HG(G) \leq f_1(\Delta)$; (ii) if $G$ is $d$-degenerate, then $HG(G) \leq f_2(d)$; (iii) if the minimum degree of $G$ is $\delta$, then $HG(G) \geq f_3(\delta)$, and $f_3(\delta)$ tends to infinity when $\delta$ tends to infinity.
rows.context_text: The authors seek to understand how basic graph parameters control the hat guessing number. The existence of $f_1$ is already known via the Lovász Local Lemma ($HG(G) < e^\Delta$), but whether $f_2$ (degeneracy bound) or $f_3$ (minimum-degree lower bound) exist is unclear. Theorems 1.6 and 1.8 provide partial progress toward part (ii).
rows.source_text: Do there exist functions $f_i : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, $1 \leq i \leq 3$ such that (i) if the maximum degree of $G$ is $\Delta$, then $HG(G) \leq f_1(\Delta)$; (ii) if $G$ is $d$-degenerate, then $HG(G) \leq f_2(d)$; (iii) if the minimum degree of $G$ is $\delta$, then $HG(G) \geq f_3(\delta)$, and $f_3(\delta)$ tends to infinity when $\delta$ tends to infinity.
rows.verification_note: Authored in X227.v:hat_guessing_degree_degeneracy_bounds_statement. Alon-Ben-Eliezer-Shangguan-Tamo Problem 1.4, the conjunction of its three parts: (i) exists f1 with HG(G) <= f1(Delta G); (ii) exists f2 with HG(G) <= f2(d) for every d-degenerate G; (iii) exists f3 with HG(G) >= f3(d) for every G of minimum degree exactly d, and f3 tending to infinity (GTBase asymptotics' eventually). The hat game is local x227 vocabulary: a strategy is one guessing function per vertex, admissible when it depends only on the colours of N(v); HG(G) >= q is x227_hat_guessing_win and HG(G) <= m is x227_hat_guess
rows.status_semantics: Problem 1.4 remains largely open. Part (i) (HG(G) bounded by a function of maximum degree) was already settled before the problem was stated via the Lovász Local Lemma. Parts (ii) and (iii) are unresolved: for part (ii), several papers have studied hat guessing numbers of degenerate and strongly degenerate graphs and shown that HG can grow at least as fast as $2^{2^{d-1}}$ for $d$-degenerate graphs, but whether an upper bound $f_2(d)$ exists is still open; for part (iii), no evidence of a minimum-degree lower bound was found.
rows.class_notes: Alon-Ben-Eliezer-Shangguan-Tamo Problem 1.4: existence of f1 (HG(G) <= f1(Delta)), f2 (HG(G) <= f2(d) for d-degenerate G) and f3 (HG(G) >= f3(delta) with f3 -> infinity). Modelling: the hat guessing number is the value of a finite perfect-information game, so it is definable as a bounded existential over guessing strategies.

rows.title: Open Problem (Section 1.1)
rows.paper_title: Baker game and polynomial-time approximation schemes
rows.statement_text: It is an open problem whether some variation on the local search approach can give PTAS for all monotone FO optimization problems.
rows.context_text: Cabello–Gajser and Har-Peled–Quanrud showed that the trivial local search algorithm (performing bounded-size changes on an initial solution as long as it can be improved) gives PTASes for maximum independent set and minimum dominating set, as well as many related problems, on classes with strongly sublinear separators. The question is whether this approach, or a variation thereof, can be extended to cover all monotone first-order optimization problems on such classes.
rows.source_text: It is an open problem whether some variation on the local search approach can give PTAS for all monotone FO optimization problems.
rows.status_semantics: The open problem asks whether a local search variation yields PTAS for all monotone first-order optimization problems on classes with strongly sublinear separators. Dvořák's follow-up work (arXiv:2103.08698, SWAT 2022) obtains PTAS for fractionally treewidth-fragile classes (which include all common strongly sublinear separator classes) and a QPTAS for all strongly sublinear separator classes, via Baker-style decomposition techniques rather than local search. The specific question about the local search approach remains unresolved, and PTAS for the full generality of strongly sublinear separator classes (beyond fractionally treewidth-fragile ones) is still open.

rows.status_semantics: The open problem of finding the asymptotic rate for moderate deviations of subgraph counts across the entire range of sparse densities in $G(n,m)$ and $G(n,p)$ remains open for general subgraphs. For triangle counts specifically, Alvarado, Gonçalves de Oliveira, and Griffiths (2023, published 2025) determined $\log\mathbb{P}(N_{\triangle}(G) > (1+\delta)p^3 n^3)$ up to a constant factor for densities above $n^{-1/2}(\log n)^{1/2}$, and also handled the lower tail for cherries. rows.title: Conjecture 1.1
rows.paper_title: Books versus triangles at the extremal density
rows.statement_text: If $n/6 \leq b < n/4$, then every graph on $n$ vertices with at least $\lfloor n^2/4 \rfloor$ edges and book number at most $b$ which is not the balanced complete bipartite graph has at least $b^2(n - 4b)$ triangles, with equality if and only if the graph is $S_{b,n}$.
rows.context_text: The authors introduce the 3-prism blow-up $S_{b,n}$ — formed by blowing up the 3-prism graph with four parts of size $b$ and two parts of size $\lfloor(n-4b)/2\rfloor$ and $\lceil(n-4b)/2\rceil$ — as the conjectured extremal construction. The conjecture implies an asymptotically tight bound on $t(n,b)$ for $n/6 \leq b \leq n/4 - \omega(1)$, fully addressing Mubayi's question about the $\gamma(\beta)$ dependency. A footnote notes the construction is essentially identical to one in an earlier arXiv version of Mubayi's paper.
rows.source_text: If $n/6 \leq b < n/4$, then every graph on $n$ vertices with at least $\lfloor n^2/4 \rfloor$ edges and book number at most $b$ which is not the balanced complete bipartite graph has at least $b^2(n - 4b)$ triangles, with equality if and only if the graph is $S_{b,n}$.
rows.status_semantics: Conjecture 1.1 remains open in full generality. The authors themselves proved it for the boundary case b = n/6 and for the near-upper-boundary range 0.2495n ≤ b < n/4, leaving the bulk of the interval n/6 < b < 0.2495n unresolved. No subsequent paper resolving the remaining cases was found in the indexed literature as of May 2026.
rows.class_notes: Fully quantified finite extremal statement; book number is standard and S_{b,n} is defined in context.

rows.title: Conjecture 1.12
rows.paper_title: Combinatorial anti-concentration inequalities, with applications
rows.statement_text: Fix $p \in (0,1)$ and fix a graph $H$ with $h$ non-isolated vertices. Let $G \in G(n,p)$. Then for any $x \in \mathbb{N}$, $$\Pr(X_H = x) = O\!\left(1/\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(X_H)}\right) = O\!\left(1/n^{h-1}\right).$$
rows.context_text: The authors establish via Corollary 1.11 that $\Pr(X_H = x) = O(1/\sqrt{r})$ where $r$ is the number of edge-disjoint copies of $H$ in $G$, giving $O(1/n)$ in $G(n,p)$, but believe this is far from optimal. The conjectured bound matches the Gaussian scale and is best-possible given the known CLT for $X_H$. Theorem 1.14 confirms the conjecture for cliques $H = K_h$.
rows.source_text: Fix $p \in (0,1)$ and fix a graph $H$ with $h$ non-isolated vertices. Let $G \in G(n,p)$. Then for any $x \in \mathbb{N}$, $$\Pr(X_H = x) = O\!\left(1/\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(X_H)}\right) = O\!\left(1/n^{h-1}\right).$$
rows.status_semantics: Conjecture 1.12 (that Pr(X_H = x) = O(1/sqrt(Var(X_H))) = O(1/n^{h-1}) for any fixed graph H with h non-isolated vertices in G(n,p)) has been resolved affirmatively for connected graphs H by Sah and Sawhney (arXiv:2006.11369, JLMS 2022), who established a local CLT for connected subgraph counts achieving the optimal scale. However, the same paper provides a counterexample showing the bound fails for certain disconnected graphs H, so the conjecture as stated for all graphs with non-isolated vertices is disproved. A companion paper (arXiv:1905.12749, Ann. Prob. 2021) by the same authors proved the near-optimal bound O(n^{1-h+o(1)}) for connected H, confirming the conjecture up to a subpolynomial factor.
rows.class_notes: Precise anti-concentration bound for subgraph counts in G(n,p); needs probability-on-graphs plus O() wrapper.

rows.title: Problem 1
rows.paper_title: Coloring count cones of planar graphs
rows.statement_text: Does there exist a polynomial-time algorithm which, given a near-triangulation $G$ with the outer face bounded by a 4-cycle $C$ and a 4-coloring $\psi$ of $C$, correctly decides whether $\psi$ extends to a 4-coloring of $G$?
rows.context_text: The authors note that even very basic precoloring extension questions for planar graphs are wide open. There exist infinitely many near-triangulations $G$ whose outer 4-cycle has a precoloring that does not extend to a 4-coloring of $G$, yet no good characterization of such graphs is known.
rows.source_text: Does there exist a polynomial-time algorithm which, given a near-triangulation $G$ with the outer face bounded by a 4-cycle $C$ and a 4-coloring $\psi$ of $C$, correctly decides whether $\psi$ extends to a 4-coloring of $G$?
rows.status_semantics: Problem 1 asks whether a polynomial-time algorithm exists to decide if a 4-coloring of the outer 4-cycle of a near-triangulation extends to the whole graph; the general question remains open. Dvořák, Moore, Seifrtová, and Šámal (arXiv:2312.13061) provide partial progress by giving linear-time algorithms for the special subclass of planar near-Eulerian-triangulations (all interior vertices have even degree) when the outer face has length at most 5, which covers the 4-cycle case within that restricted class. No resolution of the full statement for arbitrary near-triangulations was found in the literature.
rows.class_notes: Precise poly-time decision question for 4-precoloring extension on near-triangulations; also needs planarity layer.

rows.title: Conjecture 8
rows.paper_title: Coloring count cones of planar graphs
rows.statement_text: Every plane near-cubic graph $\tilde{G}$ with $d(\tilde{G}) = 5$ satisfies $n_{\tilde{G}} \in B'_5$.
rows.context_text: The cone $B'_5$ is defined as the subcone of $B_5$ spanned by the rays $\operatorname{ray}(\tilde{R}_{5,1}), \ldots, \operatorname{ray}(\tilde{R}_{5,11})$, excluding the ray corresponding to the non-planar graph $\tilde{R}_{5,12}$. By Lemma 7, membership of $n_{\tilde{G}}$ in the full cone $B_5$ is equivalent to the Four Color Theorem, so this conjecture is a strict strengthening of the Four Color Theorem. The authors verify it for all plane near-cubic graphs with fewer than 30 vertices.
rows.source_text: Every plane near-cubic graph $\tilde{G}$ with $d(\tilde{G}) = 5$ satisfies $n_{\tilde{G}} \in B'_5$.

rows.title: Conjecture 1.3
rows.paper_title: Quasi-polynomial time approximation schemes for the Maximum Weight Independent Set Problem in H-free graphs
rows.statement_text: For every forest $H$ of maximum degree at most three, MWIS admits a QPTAS and a subexponential-time algorithm in the class of graphs that do not contain any subdivision of $H$ as an induced subgraph.
rows.context_text: Following Theorems 1.1 and 1.2, which establish QPTASes and subexponential-time algorithms for MWIS in $H$-free graphs where every component of $H$ is a path or a subdivided claw, the authors conjecture a broader generalization to all forests of maximum degree at most three and graphs excluding any subdivision of $H$ as an induced subgraph. The paper itself proves Conjecture 1.3 for $H$ being a forest with at most three vertices of degree three (with a $2^{O(|V(G)|^{40/41}\log|V(G)|)}$ subexponential bound), but the full generality remains open.
rows.source_text: For every forest $H$ of maximum degree at most three, MWIS admits a QPTAS and a subexponential-time algorithm in the class of graphs that do not contain any subdivision of $H$ as an induced subgraph.
rows.class_notes: Precise algorithmic conjecture (QPTAS + subexponential MWIS in H-subdivision-free graphs); QPTAS notion needs the complexity foundation.

rows.title: Conjecture 5
rows.paper_title: Edge-partitioning 3-edge-connected graphs into paths
rows.statement_text: There is a function $f$ such that, for any fixed tree $T$ with $m$ leaves, every $f(m)$-edge-connected graph with minimum degree at least $f(|E(T)|)$ and number of edges divisible by $|E(T)|$ has a $T$-decomposition.
rows.context_text: This conjecture is posed by the paper's authors as an alternative to Conjecture 2 (which fails for trees of maximum degree three), bounding the required edge-connectivity in terms of the number of leaves of $T$ rather than its maximum degree. The paper's main result implies $f(2) = 3$ is achievable, and the authors note that establishing the existence of $f(3)$ would already contain the claw case.

rows.title: Conjecture 2
rows.paper_title: Bounding the number of cycles in a graph in terms of its degree sequence
rows.statement_text: Every simple graph with $m$ edges has at most $O(\kappa_1^m)$ cycles, where $\kappa_1 = (2+2\sqrt{2})^{1/5} \approx 1.3701$.
rows.context_text: The Arman–Tsaturian construction [2] gives simple graphs with $\Omega(\kappa_1^m)$ cycles, which is the best known lower bound. The authors verified by computer several similar constructions and could not find a better one, leading them to conjecture that this construction is optimal. Remark 9 notes that any counterexample would necessarily have average degree in the range $(4.24, 7.18)$.

rows.title: Conjecture 1
rows.paper_title: Independence number in triangle-free graphs avoiding a minor
rows.statement_text: For every positive integer $t$, if an $n$-vertex graph $G$ does not contain $K_{t+1}$ as a minor then $\alpha(G) \geq n/t$.
rows.context_text: This conjecture is a natural weakening of Hadwiger's conjecture: since Hadwiger's conjecture would imply every $n$-vertex $K_{t+1}$-minor-free graph has chromatic number at most $t$ and thus an independent set of size at least $n/t$, this bound has attracted considerable attention (see Seymour's survey [31]). Duchet and Meyniel proved the bound holds within a factor of 2 in 1982, and subsequent improvements have been made by Fox, Balogh–Kostochka, and others. The present paper studies this conjecture restricted to triangle-free graphs.

rows.title: Question 1.12
rows.paper_title: Avoidable paths in graphs
rows.statement_text: For every positive integer $k$, does every graph $G$ either not contain two disjoint $P_k$, or contain two disjoint avoidable $P_k$?
rows.context_text: The analogous statement for non-adjacent avoidable $P_k$ is established as Corollary 1.11. The authors note the answer is positive for $k \in \{1,2\}$ by results of Beisegel et al., but then provide an explicit counterexample for every $k \geq 3$ (a cycle on $2k-1$ vertices with one extra vertex adjacent to two consecutive cycle vertices), resolving the question negatively within the same paper.
rows.source_text: For every positive integer $k$, does every graph $G$ either not contain two disjoint $P_k$, or contain two disjoint avoidable $P_k$?
rows.status_semantics: Question 1.12 is resolved negatively within the same paper: the authors provide an explicit counterexample for every k >= 3 (a cycle on 2k-1 vertices with one additional vertex adjacent to two consecutive cycle vertices), showing that two disjoint P_k need not contain two disjoint avoidable P_k. The cases k in {1,2} have positive answers by results of Beisegel et al. A web search found no follow-up papers further studying this specific question.
rows.class_notes: 'Avoidable P_k' is the paper's own notion, not defined in context_text; disproved with explicit counterexample for k>=3, so right-polarity target once avoidability is defined.

rows.title: Question 4.1
rows.paper_title: Avoidable paths in graphs
rows.statement_text: Does there exist a family $\mathcal{H}$ of connected graphs, not containing any path, such that any graph is either $\mathcal{H}$-free or contains an avoidable element of $\mathcal{H}$?
rows.context_text: Having established avoidable paths of every length, the authors ask whether avoidability extends to other graph structures. They note that even allowing a family rather than a single pattern, no candidate beyond paths seems to survive tests on chordal graphs or simple ad hoc constructions, and that the notion of avoidability for non-path structures is deliberately left open to interpretation.
rows.source_text: Does there exist a family $\mathcal{H}$ of connected graphs, not containing any path, such that any graph is either $\mathcal{H}$-free or contains an avoidable element of $\mathcal{H}$?
rows.status_semantics: Question 4.1 is directly addressed by Gurvich, Krnc, Milanič, and Vyalyi in 'Avoidability beyond paths' (arXiv:2208.12803, published in Electronic Journal of Combinatorics 2025). That paper introduces a framework of two-rooted graphs to generalise avoidability beyond paths, and provides both positive and negative results about which connected non-path structures admit an avoidability property. The question is not fully resolved: no family H satisfying the exact condition of Question 4.1 is identified, but the framework clarifies structural obstructions and establishes partial answers for restricted graph classes such as C5-free graphs.
rows.defer_reason: Avoidability for non-path structures is 'deliberately left open to interpretation' per the authors; not a single well-defined proposition.

rows.title: Conjecture on polynomial-time solvability of bounded sub-determinant integer programs
rows.paper_title: The stable set problem in graphs with bounded genus and bounded odd cycle packing number
rows.statement_text: Integer programs with bounded sub-determinants can be solved in polynomial time. In particular, the stable set problem on graphs with $\mathrm{ocp}(G) \leq k$ is polynomial for every fixed $k$.
rows.context_text: The authors note that recent work links the complexity of integer programs to the magnitude of their sub-determinants, and that it is tempting to believe bounded sub-determinant integer programs are polynomial-time solvable. This would imply the stable set problem is polynomial for every fixed bound $k$ on the odd cycle packing number, which remains open for $k \geq 2$.
rows.source_text: Integer programs with bounded sub-determinants can be solved in polynomial time. In particular, the stable set problem on graphs with $\mathrm{ocp}(G) \leq k$ is polynomial for every fixed $k$.
rows.source_locator: arXiv:1908.06300 — Conjecture on polynomial-time solvability of bounded sub-determinant integer programs
rows.status_semantics: The conjecture has two components: the general claim that all bounded sub-determinant integer programs are polynomial-time solvable, and the specific claim that the stable set problem is polynomial for every fixed odd cycle packing bound $k$. The latter was settled by arXiv:2106.05947 (FOCS 2021), which gives the first polynomial-time algorithm for the weighted stable set problem on graphs with at most $k$ vertex-disjoint odd cycles for any constant $k$, extending the previously known cases $k=0$ (bipartite) and $k=1$. The broader claim about all bounded sub-determinant IPs remains open in full generality; known positive results cover bimodular matrices and matrices with at most two nonzero entries per row.

rows.title: Conjecture 3.1
rows.paper_title: Disproportionate division
rows.statement_text: For any $n \geq 2$ non-atomic probability measures $\mu_1, \mu_2, \ldots, \mu_n$ on the unit circle $S^1$ and non-negative reals $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n$ summing to $1$, there exists a partition of the set $[n] = P \cup Q$ into two nonempty sets and a partition of the circle $S^1 = X \cup X^c$ into two intervals such that $$\min_{i \in P} \mu_i(X) = \sum_{j \in P} \alpha_j \quad \text{and} \quad \min_{i \in Q} \mu_i(X^c) = \sum_{j \in Q} \alpha_j.$$
rows.context_text: The authors introduce this conjecture as a topological measure-partitioning statement whose truth would imply, by a simple inductive argument, that $f(n) = 2n-2$ for all $n \geq 2$, which would be optimal for disproportionate division. The $n=2$ case is known and is essentially the Stromquist–Woodall theorem, but the conjecture is open already for $n=3$.

rows.title: Classical MIS Dichotomy Conjecture
rows.paper_title: When Maximum Stable Set can be solved in FPT time
rows.statement_text: For every connected graph $H$, Maximum Independent Set in $H$-free graphs is in $\mathsf{P}$ if and only if $H \in \{P_\ell\}_{\ell} \cup \{S_{i,j,k}\}_{i \leq j \leq k}$.
rows.context_text: The polynomial-time complexity of MIS in $H$-free graphs has been studied since the early 1980s. Alekseev showed that if $H$ is neither a path nor a subdivided claw then MIS is NP-complete on $H$-free graphs, motivating this conjecture about the full dichotomy. The authors note that an even stronger conjecture is postulated by Lozin [28].
rows.source_text: For every connected graph $H$, Maximum Independent Set in $H$-free graphs is in $\mathsf{P}$ if and only if $H \in \{P_\ell\}_{\ell} \cup \{S_{i,j,k}\}_{i \leq j \leq k}$.
rows.status_semantics: The conjecture that MIS in H-free graphs is in P if and only if H is a path or subdivided claw remains open at the polynomial-time level. The landmark post-2019 development is arXiv:2305.15738 (Gartland, Lokshtanov, Masařík, M. Pilipczuk, M. Pilipczuk, Rzążewski; STOC 2024), which proves MWIS is solvable in quasi-polynomial time for every H-free graph class where H is a path or subdivided claw, closing the gap between predicted-tractable cases and NP-hardness. Polynomial-time algorithms are established for specific subclasses (P_t-free for t ≤ 6, fork-free/S_{1,1,2}-free), but polynomial-time solvability for all S_{i,j,k}-free graphs remains open.

rows.title: Parameterized MIS Dichotomy
rows.paper_title: When Maximum Stable Set can be solved in FPT time
rows.statement_text: Is MIS (randomized) FPT or $W[1]$-hard in $H$-free graphs?
rows.context_text: This is the parameterized counterpart of the classical MIS dichotomy question. Alekseev's NP-hardness reduction does not transfer to $W[1]$-hardness, leaving a priori more candidate graphs $H$ for which the parameterized status is open. Dabrowski et al. initiated a systematic study of this question.
rows.source_text: Is MIS (randomized) FPT or $W[1]$-hard in $H$-free graphs?
rows.status_semantics: The full FPT vs W[1]-hard dichotomy for MIS in H-free graphs remains open as of 2026. Significant partial progress has been made: the dichotomy is completely resolved for all 4-vertex forbidden subgraphs, and many 5-vertex cases are settled, but cases such as P7-free, S_{1,1,3}-free, and S_{1,2,2}-free graphs remain open. A 2020 follow-up by Dvořák et al. strengthened hardness results by proving parameterized inapproximability lower bounds under ETH/Gap-ETH for graph classes where W[1]-hardness was already known, without resolving new FPT cases.

Nguyen, Scott, and Seymour (arXiv:2312.15572, 2023) proved that for every d > 0, every n-vertex graph of VC-dimension at most d contains a clique or stable set of size at least n^c for an explicit constant c > 0 depending only on d, with the bound c_d ≥ 2^{-2^{O(d)}}. rows.title: Conjecture 2.2
rows.paper_title: Maximum independent sets in (pyramid, even hole)-free graphs
rows.statement_text: There is a polynomial $P$ such that every graph $G$ that contains no prism, pyramid, theta or turtle has at most $P(|V(G)|)$ minimal separators.
rows.context_text: The authors survey families of graphs with exponentially many minimal separators (k-prisms, k-pyramids, k-thetas, k-turtles, k-ladders) and observe that every known such example contains a prism, pyramid, theta, or turtle. They propose Conjecture 2.2 as 'in some sense the best possible statement regarding bounding the number of minimal separators.' The paper proves a weaker result (Theorem 2.3) for the class $\mathcal{C}$ of (square, prism, pyramid, theta, even wheel)-free graphs.
rows.source_text: There is a polynomial $P$ such that every graph $G$ that contains no prism, pyramid, theta or turtle has at most $P(|V(G)|)$ minimal separators.
rows.status_semantics: Conjecture 2.2 from arXiv:1912.11246 was proved in full by Abrishami, Chudnovsky, Dibek, Thomassé, Trotignon, and Vušković in arXiv:2005.05042. Their Theorem 1.2 establishes that every (theta, pyramid, prism, turtle)-free graph G has at most |V(G)|^18 minimal separators, constructible in polynomial time. The result is optimal in the sense that excluding only three of the four forbidden subgraphs still permits exponentially many minimal separators.

rows.status_semantics: The complexity of maximum independent set in even-hole-free graphs (polynomial-time vs. NP-hard) remains open. Significant partial progress has been made: Abrishami et al. (arXiv:2005.05042, 2020) give a polynomial-time MWIS algorithm for (theta, pyramid, prism, turtle)-free graphs, subsuming the (pyramid, even hole)-free result. More decisively, Chudnovsky, Gartland, Hajebi, Lokshtanov, and Spirkl (arXiv:2407.08927, 2024) prove that every n-vertex even-hole-free graph has tree independence number at most c·log^{10}(n), yielding a quasi-polynomial time algorithm for MWIS across the full even-hole-free class—a major advance that nonetheless leaves the polynomial vs. NP-hard question unresolved.

rows.title: Problem 3
rows.paper_title: An update on reconfiguring $10$-colorings of planar graphs
rows.statement_text: What is the minimum integer $\kappa$ such that for every planar graph $G$ with $n$ vertices, $R_{\kappa}(G)$ has diameter $O(n)$?
rows.context_text: Planar graphs are 5-degenerate and have maximum average degree less than 6; prior results give $R_8(G)$ diameter $O(n(\log n)^7)$ and $R_{12}(G)$ diameter at most $6n$ for planar $G$. The paper improves the upper bound to $\kappa \leq 10$ via Theorem 4, and an isolated 6-coloring of the icosahedron shows $\kappa \geq 7$; the authors note that $\kappa = 7$ cannot be excluded.
rows.source_text: What is the minimum integer $\kappa$ such that for every planar graph $G$ with $n$ vertices, $R_{\kappa}(G)$ has diameter $O(n)$?
rows.status_semantics: Problem 3 asks for the minimum $\kappa$ such that $R_\kappa(G)$ has diameter $O(n)$ for every $n$-vertex planar graph $G$. The source paper establishes $7 \leq \kappa \leq 10$. rows.title: The $\varepsilon$-$t$-Net Problem
rows.paper_title: The $ε$-$t$-Net Problem
rows.statement_text: How small are the smallest $\varepsilon$-$t$-nets for $H$? Can we compute them efficiently?
rows.context_text: Given a finite hypergraph $H=(V,E)$, a positive integer $t$, and $\varepsilon\in(t/|V|,1)$, an $\varepsilon$-$t$-net is a family $S\subseteq\binom{V}{t}$ of $t$-element subsets of $V$ such that every hyperedge $e\in E$ with $|e|\geq\varepsilon|V|$ contains some $s\in S$. The problem generalises the classical $\varepsilon$-net problem ($t=1$) and the Mnet notion ($t=\Theta(\varepsilon|V|)$), and arises naturally in secret sharing and other combinatorial contexts.

rows.title: Conjecture 1.2
rows.paper_title: A universal exponent for homeomorphs
rows.statement_text: For each 3-graph $H$, there exists $C_H > 0$ such that any 3-graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with at least $C_H n^{5/2}$ edges contains a homeomorph of $H$.
rows.context_text: The paper proves the exponent $3-1/5$ is universal but does not believe it to be tight. The conjectured optimal exponent $5/2 = 3 - 1/2$ is motivated by the Brown–Erdős–Sós result that $5/2$ is the correct exponent for the sphere $S^2$ (i.e., $K^3_4$), and by the analogy that homeomorphs in 3-graphs should appear roughly once spheres (homeomorphs of $S^2$) can be found, just as homeomorphs in graphs appear roughly once cycles (homeomorphs of $S^1$) can be found.
rows.source_text: For each 3-graph $H$, there exists $C_H > 0$ such that any 3-graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with at least $C_H n^{5/2}$ edges contains a homeomorph of $H$.
rows.status_semantics: Conjecture 1.2 posits that the optimal exponent for homeomorphs of any fixed 3-graph $H$ is $5/2$; the source paper itself establishes the weaker universal bound $3-1/5 \approx 2.8$. Maya Sankar (2024) subsequently improved this upper bound to $8/3 \approx 2.667$ for all 2-dimensional simplicial complexes, bringing it closer to the conjectured optimum. The full conjecture remains open.

rows.title: Algorithm Termination Conjecture
rows.paper_title: Pentagon contact representations
rows.statement_text: We conjecture that the algorithm always terminates.
rows.context_text: The paper proposes an algorithm for computing homothetic pentagon contact representations based on systems of linear equations derived from five color forests. When the solution is non-negative it encodes distances between pentagon corners and the representation is constructed; otherwise negative variables guide a local change of the five color forest and the procedure restarts. The authors note that a proof of this conjecture would yield an existence proof for pentagon contact representations independent of Schramm's Monster Packing Theorem. Analogous algorithms for homothetic triangle and square contact representations exist but also lack termination proofs.

rows.title: Problem 3
rows.paper_title: Asymmetric list sizes in bipartite graphs
rows.statement_text: Given $\Delta_A$ and $\Delta_B$, what are optimal choices of $k_A \leq \Delta_A$ and $k_B \leq \Delta_B$ for which any bipartite graph $G = (V = A \cup B, E)$ with parts $A$ and $B$ having maximum degrees at most $\Delta_A$ and $\Delta_B$, respectively, is $(k_A, k_B)$-choosable?
rows.context_text: The authors introduce $(k_A, k_B)$-choosability as an asymmetric generalisation of ordinary list colouring of bipartite graphs, where vertices in part $A$ receive lists of size $k_A$ and vertices in part $B$ receive lists of size $k_B$. Problem 3 asks for the optimal list-size pairs in terms of the one-sided maximum degrees $\Delta_A$ and $\Delta_B$, and subsumes Conjecture 2 as its symmetric special case.

rows.defer_reason: 'What are optimal choices of k_A, k_B' asks for optimal parameter pairs, not a single proposition.
rows.class_notes: Asymmetric generalization of the matched OPG bipartite list-chromatic problem (subsumes its symmetric Conjecture 2).

rows.title: Conjecture 7
rows.paper_title: Asymmetric list sizes in bipartite graphs
rows.statement_text:
Let the positive integers $\Delta_A, \Delta_B, k_A, k_B$ satisfy one of the following.
(i) Given $\varepsilon > 0$, we have $\Delta_A, \Delta_B \geq \Delta_0$ for some $\Delta_0 = \Delta_0(\varepsilon)$, and $k_A \geq \Delta_A^\varepsilon$ and $k_B \geq \Delta_B^\varepsilon$.
(ii) For some absolute constant $C > 1$, $k_A \geq C \log \Delta_B$ and $k_B \geq C \log \Delta_A$.
(iii) $\Delta_A = \Delta_B = \Delta$, and, for some absolute constant $C > 0$, $k_B \geq C(\Delta/\log\Delta)^{1/k_A} \log\Delta$ or $k_A \geq C(\Delta/\log\Delta)^{1/k_B} \log\Delta$.
Then any bipartite graph $G = (V = A \cup B, E)$ with parts $A$ and $B$ having maximum degrees at most $\Delta_A$ and $\Delta_B$, respectively, is $(k_A, k_B)$-choosable.
rows.context_text: Motivated by the asymptotic behaviour of $(k_A, k_B)$-choosability for complete bipartite graphs (Theorem 6 and Theorem 16), the authors conjecture three concrete asymmetric analogues of the Krivelevich–Alon conjecture. Condition (i) is weaker than Conjecture 2; conditions (ii) and (iii) are stronger. The paper shows Conjecture 7 holds for complete bipartite graphs (Theorem 15) and provides partial progress in the general case via Theorem 4 and its corollaries.

rows.title: Conjecture 5 (Improved Approximation Conjecture)
rows.paper_title: An algorithmic weakening of the Erdős-Hajnal conjecture
rows.statement_text: Every graph $H$ satisfies the improved approximation property, i.e., there exists a constant $\varepsilon > 0$ such that MIS admits a (randomized) $n^{1-\varepsilon}$-approximation polynomial algorithm on every $H$-free $n$-vertex graph $G$.
rows.context_text: This conjecture is introduced as an algorithmic weakening of the Erdős-Hajnal conjecture. It states informally that the inapproximability of MIS in general graphs can always be beaten in any proper hereditary class. It is strictly weaker than the Erdős-Hajnal conjecture, since MIS is polynomial in $P_6$-free graphs while it is open whether $P_5$ satisfies the Erdős-Hajnal property.
rows.source_text: Every graph $H$ satisfies the improved approximation property, i.e., there exists a constant $\varepsilon > 0$ such that MIS admits a (randomized) $n^{1-\varepsilon}$-approximation polynomial algorithm on every $H$-free $n$-vertex graph $G$.
rows.class_notes: Single proposition (every H has the n^{1-eps}-approximation property for MIS on H-free graphs); algorithmic weakening of Erdos–Hajnal.

rows.title: Question (common superclass for FPT FO model checking)
rows.paper_title: Twin-width I: tractable FO model checking
rows.statement_text: Do bounded twin-width and nowhere dense classes admit a natural common superclass still admitting an FPT algorithm for FO model checking?
rows.context_text: Figure 3 shows that bounded twin-width and nowhere dense classes together roughly subsume all current knowledge on fixed-parameter tractability of FO model checking. The authors explicitly pose whether a natural common superclass of both still admits an FPT algorithm for FO model checking.
rows.source_text: Do bounded twin-width and nowhere dense classes admit a natural common superclass still admitting an FPT algorithm for FO model checking?
rows.source_locator: arXiv:2004.14789 — Question (common superclass for FPT FO model checking)
rows.status_semantics: The natural candidate common superclass — monadically NIP (monadically dependent) classes — has been identified in the literature and is known to contain both bounded twin-width and nowhere dense classes. Significant partial progress has been made: FPT FO model checking was proved for all monadically stable graph classes (which strictly contain all nowhere dense classes) in 2023, and for all classes of bounded merge-width (which unify bounded twin-width and bounded expansion) in 2025. The full question of whether all monadically NIP/dependent classes admit FPT FO model checking remains an open conjecture, widely regarded as the central problem in the area.
rows.defer_reason: Asks for a 'natural common superclass' — open-ended search for a class, not a proposition.

rows.title: Conjecture 1.4
rows.paper_title: Graphs with polynomially many minimal separators
rows.statement_text: There exists $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that if no induced subgraph of $G$ is a $k$-creature, then $G$ has at most $|V(G)|^{f(k)}$ minimal separators.
rows.context_text: A $k$-creature is a graph whose vertex set partitions into sets $A, B, \{x_1,\ldots,x_k\}, \{y_1,\ldots,y_k\}$ satisfying connectivity, anticomplete, and matching conditions; every $k$-creature contains a theta, pyramid, prism, or turtle. The authors propose this as a stronger generalisation of Theorem 1.2, noting that even if true it does not fully characterise classes with the polynomial separator property (the class $\mathcal{D}$ of induced subgraphs of $k$-turtles with very long paths has the polynomial separator property yet contains $k$-creatures of arbitrarily large $k$).
rows.source_text: There exists $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that if no induced subgraph of $G$ is a $k$-creature, then $G$ has at most $|V(G)|^{f(k)}$ minimal separators.
rows.status_semantics: Conjecture 1.4 was disproved by Gartland and Lokshtanov (arXiv:2007.08761, posted July 2020), who exhibited a counterexample showing that forbidding k-creatures for a fixed k does not suffice to guarantee polynomially many minimal separators. Their paper proves instead the weaker result that hereditary classes excluding k-creatures are 'strongly quasi-tame' (quasi-polynomially many minimal separators) under an additional condition that minimal separators can be dominated by a bounded number of vertices. Related SODA 2023 work showed that forbidding both k-creatures and k-critters yields a quasi-polynomial separator bound.
rows.class_notes: k-creature only sketched in context ('connectivity, anticomplete, and matching conditions' unspecified); disproved, so right-polarity target once recovered.

rows.title: Conjecture 1.10
rows.paper_title: Many flows in the group connectivity setting
rows.statement_text: There exists a fixed constant $c > 1$ so that the following holds. For every 3-edge-connected oriented graph $G = (V, E)$ of order $n$, every abelian group $\Gamma$ with $|\Gamma| \geq 6$, and every $f : E \to \Gamma$, there exist at least $c^n$ flows $\phi : E \to \Gamma$ with $\phi(e) \neq f(e)$ for every $e \in E$.
rows.context_text: Theorem 1.9 establishes an explicit exponential lower bound on the number of $\Gamma$-connected flows for groups of size $k \geq 8$, but yields only the existence of a single flow for $k = 6, 7$. The authors attribute this gap to a shortcoming of their techniques and conjecture the exponential bound holds for all abelian groups of size at least 6. Theorem 1.9 confirms the conjecture for all groups except $\mathbb{Z}_6$ and $\mathbb{Z}_7$; Theorem 1.11 gives a superpolynomial (but not exponential) lower bound for $\mathbb{Z}_6$.
rows.source_text: There exists a fixed constant $c > 1$ so that the following holds. For every 3-edge-connected oriented graph $G = (V, E)$ of order $n$, every abelian group $\Gamma$ with $|\Gamma| \geq 6$, and every $f : E \to \Gamma$, there exist at least $c^n$ flows $\phi : E \to \Gamma$ with $\phi(e) \neq f(e)$ for every $e \in E$.

rows.title: Question 1.5
rows.paper_title: Finding an induced path that is not a shortest path
rows.statement_text: For fixed $k > 1$, is there a polynomial-time algorithm that, given a graph $G$ and $u, v \in V(G)$, decides whether there is an induced $uv$-path $P$ in $G$ of length at least $d(u, v) + k$?
rows.context_text: The paper's main result (Theorem 1.1) gives a polynomial-time algorithm for the case $k = 1$ (detecting any induced non-shortest path), and the authors note the algorithm can be adjusted for $k = 2$. The question remains open even for $k = 3$. Fixing $k$ is necessary, since Theorem 1.6 shows the problem is NP-hard when $k$ is part of the input (e.g., deciding whether there exists a $uv$-NSP of length at least $2d_G(u,v)$).
rows.source_text: For fixed $k > 1$, is there a polynomial-time algorithm that, given a graph $G$ and $u, v \in V(G)$, decides whether there is an induced $uv$-path $P$ in $G$ of length at least $d(u, v) + k$?
rows.defer_reason: computation-model layer out of scope for the X211-X229 waves: GTBase.complexity's cost-coupled prog/pcost core only supports positive 'there is a polynomial-time algorithm' claims, and the 2026-07-17 blocked-retargeting audit (meta/BLOCKED_RETARGETING_AUDIT.md) rejected 48/72 of the finite-witness encodings of poly-time / NP-hardness / dichotomy rows as unfaithful.

rows.statement_text: We have that $T(n) = \widetilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{n})$. More generally, we have that $T(G) = \widetilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{|G|})$.

rows.title: Conjecture 5
rows.paper_title: A Thomassen-type method for planar graph recoloring
rows.statement_text: If $G$ is a planar graph of girth at least five on $n$ vertices, then $R_6(G)$ has diameter $O(n)$.
rows.context_text: Planar graphs of girth at least five are 2-degenerate and can be colored from lists of size three; combining Lemma 2 with Theorem 1 already shows 7 colors suffice for linear diameter. The authors believe this bound can be improved to 6, and suspect that a variation of their Thomassen-type method can be used to prove the conjecture, though several complications arise.
rows.source_text: If $G$ is a planar graph of girth at least five on $n$ vertices, then $R_6(G)$ has diameter $O(n)$.
rows.status_semantics: Conjecture 5 (that $R_6(G)$ has diameter $O(n)$ for planar graphs of girth at least five on $n$ vertices) appears to remain open in full generality. A directly relevant follow-up, arXiv:2112.00631 (SIAM J. Discrete Math. 37(1), 2023), addresses exactly the same setting and proves that the 4-recolouring graph of every planar graph of girth five is connected via a discharging argument, as well as diameter theorems for the recolouring graph; whether the $R_6$ linear-diameter statement is among those results could not be confirmed from the abstract alone, so the conjecture is classified as partially addressed.
rows.class_notes: R_6(G) is the standard 6-recoloring reconfiguration graph (buildable primitive); diameter O(n) needs a constant wrapper plus planarity/girth hypotheses.

rows.title: The Small Conjecture
rows.paper_title: Twin-width II: small classes
rows.statement_text: Every small hereditary class has bounded twin-width.
rows.context_text: The paper proves that every bounded twin-width class is small (has at most $n! c^n$ labeled $n$-vertex graphs for some constant $c$), unifying results for bounded treewidth, proper subclasses of permutation graphs, and proper minor-closed classes. The small conjecture posits the converse. The authors explore it by verifying bounded twin-width for many natural small hereditary classes that could serve as counterexamples, including subdivisions of $K_n$, graphs of bounded stack or queue number, and cubic expanders from iterated random 2-lifts.
rows.source_text: Every small hereditary class has bounded twin-width.
rows.verification_note: Authored in X220.v:small_hereditary_class_bounded_twin_width_statement. Bonnet-Geniet-Kim-Thomasse-Watrigant Twin-width II, the Small Conjecture. Twin-width is encoded by CONTRACTION SEQUENCES in partition form (x220_twin_width_le): the trigraph reached is determined by the partition, a pair of parts being red exactly when it is neither complete nor anticomplete, the sequence running from the singleton partition to a partition with at most one part (which also covers the empty graph) with red degree always at most d. A class is a Prop on sgraph; hereditary = isomorphism-closed and closed under
rows.status_semantics: The Small Conjecture ('every small hereditary class has bounded twin-width') was disproved by Bonnet, Geniet, Tessera, and Thomassé in Twin-width VII (arXiv:2204.12330, 2022), who constructed a family of induced subgraphs of an infinite Cayley graph that is small (as labeled graphs) yet has unbounded twin-width. Prior to the disproof, Twin-width IV (arXiv:2102.03117, 2021) established a positive resolution in the restricted setting of hereditary classes of ordered graphs, where bounded twin-width and smallness (growth at most 2^{O(n)}) are equivalent.
rows.class_notes: RECOVERED from arXiv:2006.09877 (Bonnet-Geniet-Kim-Thomasse-Watrigant, 'Twin-width II'): a class C is SMALL if there is a constant c such that C contains at most n! c^n graphs on the labelled vertex set [n], for every n (counted up to equality, NOT up to isomorphism); twin-width is the least d admitting a d-contraction-sequence of trigraphs of red degree at most d. The SMALL CONJECTURE (verbatim): 'Every small hereditary class has bounded twin-width' -- the converse of the paper's theorem that bounded twin-width implies small. The hereditary hypothesis is essential (dropping it gives a trivial counterexample). Recorded upstream as disproved.

rows.paper_title: Twin-width II: small classes
rows.statement_text: Do classes with polynomial expansion have bounded twin-width?
rows.context_text: Towards the small conjecture, the authors identify showing that small sparse classes have bounded (sparse) twin-width as a first, challenging step. Since classes with polynomial expansion are small, confirming bounded twin-width for them would constitute meaningful progress.

rows.title: Informal conjecture on MIS approximability vs. Min Dominating Set
rows.paper_title: Twin-width III: Max Independent Set, Min Dominating Set, and Coloring
rows.statement_text: Max Independent Set may have a very different approximability status than Min Dominating Set on bounded twin-width graphs.
rows.context_text: Theorem 6 establishes $O(1)$-approximation algorithms for Min Dominating Set and Min $r$-Dominating Set on bounded twin-width graphs, but Max Independent Set (Distance-1 MIS) is explicitly excluded from that theorem. The authors note further that a constant approximation for Max Independent Set on bounded twin-width graphs with arbitrarily large clique number would imply a PTAS, and they give some evidence that MIS sits in a fundamentally different approximability regime.
rows.source_text: Max Independent Set may have a very different approximability status than Min Dominating Set on bounded twin-width graphs.
rows.source_locator: arXiv:2007.14161 — Informal conjecture on MIS approximability vs. Min Dominating Set
rows.status_semantics: The 2022/2023 paper by Bergé, Bonnet, Déprés, and Watrigant (arXiv:2207.07708, STACS 2023) directly addresses MIS approximability on bounded twin-width graphs, establishing a polynomial-time n^ε-approximation algorithm and a time–approximation tradeoff (O(1)^{2^q-1}-approximation in time exp(O_q(n^{2^{-q}}))). This confirms that MIS sits in a strictly worse approximability regime than Min Dominating Set (which admits an O(1)-approximation) on bounded twin-width graphs, supporting the conjecture. However, no hardness result ruling out a constant-factor approximation for MIS on bounded twin-width has been established, so the precise approximability boundary remains open.
rows.defer_reason: 'May have a very different approximability status' — informal comparison, not a proposition.

rows.title: Conjecture 1.2
rows.paper_title: Automorphism groups of maps in linear time
rows.statement_text: There is no $\varepsilon > 0$ for which there is an algorithm for testing isomorphism of maps of unrestricted genus in time $O(n^{2-\varepsilon})$.
rows.context_text: The best known algorithm for the simultaneous conjugation problem runs in time $O(n^2 \log d / \log n + dn \log n)$, yielding an $O(n^2/\log n)$ algorithm for map isomorphism and automorphism problems of unrestricted genus. In complexity theory this is not considered 'truly subquadratic', which motivates the conjecture.

rows.title: Question 4.1
rows.paper_title: A note on deterministic zombies
rows.statement_text: For every graph $G$, and for a graph $G'$ obtained from $G$ by successively adding vertices of degree 1, does it always hold that $z(G') = z(G)$?
rows.context_text: This question asks whether attaching pendant vertices (leaves) to a graph leaves its zombie number unchanged. It can be interpreted as asking whether zombies can benefit from waiting at a designated position before activating at the start of the game.
rows.source_text: For every graph $G$, and for a graph $G'$ obtained from $G$ by successively adding vertices of degree 1, does it always hold that $z(G') = z(G)$?
rows.class_notes: Zombie number z(G) is the deterministic zombies-and-survivors game parameter — not defined in context but standard in that literature; needs game primitive.

rows.title: Question 4.2
rows.paper_title: A note on deterministic zombies
rows.statement_text: For any graph $G$, is there an integer $k$ such that, for $G'_k$ the graph obtained from $G$ by subdividing all edges $k$ times then adding the original edges, $z(G'_k) > z(G) + 1$?
rows.context_text: This question probes how iterated edge subdivision combined with re-adding the original edges affects the zombie number. The authors remark that $k = 5$ may be a valid universal answer for any graph $G$.

rows.title: Conjecture 2
rows.paper_title: On the tree-width of even-hole-free graphs
rows.statement_text: There is a function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that every even-hole-free graph of degree at most $d$ has tree-width at most $f(d)$.
rows.context_text: The class of even-hole-free graphs has unbounded tree-width in general (e.g., complete graphs and chordal graphs). Bounded degree is conjectured to be a sufficient structural restriction. If true, it would imply that even-hole-freeness is testable with constant query complexity and polylogarithmic running time in the bounded-degree graph model, via CMSO testability on bounded tree-width graphs. The paper proves the conjecture for $d \leq 3$ (subcubic graphs) and proves a weakening for $d = 4$.
rows.source_text: There is a function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that every even-hole-free graph of degree at most $d$ has tree-width at most $f(d)$.
rows.verification_note: Authored in X27.v:bounded_degree_even_hole_free_bounded_treewidth_statement. Encodes the even-hole-free bounded-treewidth theorem row as a function f with treewidth at most f(d) for graphs of degree at most d.
rows.status_semantics: Conjecture 2 from arXiv:2008.05504 — that every even-hole-free graph of degree at most $d$ has tree-width at most $f(d)$ for some function $f$ — was resolved affirmatively within weeks of being posted. Abrishami, Chudnovsky, and Vušković (arXiv:2009.01297, submitted September 2020) proved the full statement by showing that decomposition cutsets in even-hole-free bounded-degree graphs can be organized into a bounded number of well-behaved collections, yielding bounded treewidth. The internal reference arXiv:2108.01162 addresses a related but distinct conjecture about unavoidable induced subgraphs in bounded-degree graphs; arXiv:2507.06169 provides a counterexample to a different conjecture of Trotignon about outerstring induced subgraphs, not to Conjecture 2.
rows.class_notes: Even-hole-free + max degree d implies treewidth at most f(d); solved (Abrishami-Chudnovsky-Vuskovic line).

rows.title: Conjecture 3
rows.paper_title: On the tree-width of even-hole-free graphs
rows.statement_text: For every $d \in \mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f_d : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that every graph with degree at most $d$ and tree-width at least $f_d(k)$ contains a $(k \times k)$-wall or the line graph of a $(k \times k)$-wall as an induced subgraph.
rows.context_text: This is an induced grid theorem analogue for bounded-degree graphs, motivated by the construction of (even hole, $K_4$)-free graphs of unbounded tree-width that requires vertices of large degree and large clique minors. The conjecture is described as 'wide open' and formally implies Conjecture 2. The paper's Theorem 1.1 (the induced grid theorem for minor-free graphs) can be seen as a step in the direction of its proof.
rows.source_text: For every $d \in \mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f_d : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that every graph with degree at most $d$ and tree-width at least $f_d(k)$ contains a $(k \times k)$-wall or the line graph of a $(k \times k)$-wall as an induced subgraph.

'Treewidth at least r' is tw_ge (a lower bound on every admissible width, the X201 device); induce

Prior partial progress by Abrishami, Chudnovsky, Dibek, Hajebi, and Rzążewski (arXiv:2108.01162) established the conclusion for $S_{t,t,t}$-free graphs and $(t$-theta, $t$-pyramid)-free graphs of bounded degree and large treewidth.

rows.title: Conjecture 11
rows.paper_title: Coloring Drawings of Graphs
rows.statement_text: If $G$ is a universally cell 3-colorable graph which does not have a subcontraction isomorphic to $K^+_{3,n-3}$ for some $n \geq 7$, then $G$ is 3-flowable.
rows.context_text: The paper exhibits an infinite family of universally cell 3-colorable graphs ($K^+_{3,n-3}$ for $n \geq 7$) that do not admit a nowhere-zero 3-flow, showing the two properties are not equivalent in general. The authors believe excluding these graphs as subcontractions is sufficient to recover equivalence between universal cell 3-colorability and 3-flowability. Remarkably, a positive resolution of this conjecture would also imply Tutte's 3-Flow Conjecture.
rows.source_text: If $G$ is a universally cell 3-colorable graph which does not have a subcontraction isomorphic to $K^+_{3,n-3}$ for some $n \geq 7$, then $G$ is 3-flowable.
rows.class_notes: 'Universally cell 3-colorable' and K^+_{3,n-3} are paper-local and undefined in context; a positive resolution would imply Tutte's 3-flow conjecture.

rows.title: Conjecture 5
rows.paper_title: On a conjecture by Anthony Hill
rows.statement_text: The crossing number of $M_{n,t}$ is equal to $$H(n) - \frac{1}{2}\,t(k-1)(k-2),$$ where $k = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$.
rows.context_text: Here $M_{n,t}$ denotes the graph obtained from $K_n$ by removing a matching of size $t$, and $k = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$. Corollary 4 shows that geodesic drawings of $M_{n,t}$ built from sets of strength $0$ achieve this crossing count; the existence of many such sets of strength $0$ motivates the conjecture that this value is optimal.
rows.source_text: The crossing number of $M_{n,t}$ is equal to $$H(n) - \frac{1}{2}\,t(k-1)(k-2),$$ where $k = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$.
rows.defer_reason: Crossing number is not modelled by GTBase.surface (rotation systems give embeddings, not crossings) and needs a plane-drawings layer; the only corpus edge (e128) goes to opg:the_crossing_number_of_the_complete_graph, whose own statement is only 'partial', so no same-paper companion could be authored alongside it.
rows.class_notes: H(n) is the standard Harary-Hill value for cr(K_n); M_{n,t} = K_n minus a size-t matching is defined in context.

rows.title: Open Problem: Finding a Shortest Even Hole
rows.paper_title: Detecting a long even hole
rows.statement_text: Finding a shortest even hole in a graph (if one exists).
rows.context_text: After surveying polynomial-time algorithms for detecting even holes, the authors note that finding a shortest even hole remains open: "Another is finding a shortest even hole if there is one; this we have not yet been able to solve." This is posed as an analogue of the result of Chudnovsky, Scott and Seymour [8] that finds a shortest odd hole in $O(|G|^{14})$ time.
rows.source_text: Finding a shortest even hole in a graph (if one exists).
rows.source_locator: arXiv:2009.05691 — Open Problem: Finding a Shortest Even Hole
rows.status_semantics: The problem of finding a shortest even hole in polynomial time was resolved by Cheong and Lu in a paper posted to arXiv on August 15, 2020 — roughly one month before Cook and Seymour posed it as an open problem — giving an O(n^31) algorithm; Chiu, Lai, and Lu subsequently improved this to O(n^23) in July 2022.
rows.class_notes: Statement is a task phrase, not a proposition; intended claim (poly-time algorithm for shortest even hole) is clear from context but needs restatement; now solved.

rows.title: Open Question: Detecting Holes of Length Divisible by Three
rows.paper_title: Detecting a long even hole
rows.statement_text: Can holes whose length is a multiple of three be detected in polynomial time?
rows.context_text: Having focused on even and odd holes, the authors remark: "what about holes of length a multiple of three, can we detect them in polynomial time? Triangle-free graphs with no holes of length a multiple of three have some very interesting properties [9], but we currently have no idea how to recognize such graphs." This suggests the problem of recognising graphs with no hole of length $\equiv 0 \pmod{3}$ as a natural next direction.

rows.title: Informal Conjecture (§1.2, Theorem 1.1 remarks)
rows.paper_title: Typical and Extremal Aspects of Friends-and-Strangers Graphs
rows.statement_text: The threshold for $\mathrm{FS}(X, Y)$ to be connected when $X, Y \sim G(n,p)$ is determined by the isolated-vertex threshold: ``it seems that (as in the usual case of a binomial random graph) this local obstruction to connectedness tells essentially the whole story.''
rows.context_text: Theorem 1.1 establishes a lower bound $p \leq (2^{-1/2}-\varepsilon)/n^{1/2}$ arising from isolated vertices and an upper bound $p \geq \exp(2(\log n)^{2/3})/n^{1/2}$ for the high-probability connectivity threshold of $\mathrm{FS}(X,Y)$. The authors suggest the gap between these bounds is an artifact of the proof method and that the two thresholds should coincide up to lower-order factors.
rows.source_text: The threshold for $\mathrm{FS}(X, Y)$ to be connected when $X, Y \sim G(n,p)$ is determined by the isolated-vertex threshold: ``it seems that (as in the usual case of a binomial random graph) this local obstruction to connectedness tells essentially the whole story.''
rows.status_semantics: Three follow-up papers have narrowed the gap in Theorem 1.1 of the source paper. Milojevic (arXiv:2210.03864, 2022) improved the isolated-vertex lower bound and disproved two formal conjectures from the source paper about threshold probabilities. Krishnan and Li (arXiv:2410.21334, 2024) established k-connectivity for p ≥ n^{-1/2+o(1)}, bringing the connectivity upper bound and isolated-vertex lower bound to the same asymptotic order n^{-1/2+o(1)}, broadly consistent with the informal conjecture. A sharp threshold matching an exact constant has not been proved.
rows.defer_reason: 'Tells essentially the whole story' / thresholds coincide 'up to lower-order factors' — informal, no precise proposition.

rows.title: Open Question (§1.2, Theorem 1.4 remarks)
rows.paper_title: Typical and Extremal Aspects of Friends-and-Strangers Graphs
rows.statement_text: Do the cutoff for $\mathrm{FS}(X, Y)$ to avoid isolated vertices and the cutoff for $\mathrm{FS}(X, Y)$ to have exactly 2 connected components coincide when $r \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$? That is, is $d_{r,r} = \lceil (3r+1)/4 \rceil$ for all $r \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$?
rows.context_text: Theorem 1.4 proves $\lceil (3r+1)/4 \rceil \leq d_{r,r} \leq \lceil (3r+2)/4 \rceil$; the two bounds differ by 1 exactly when $r \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$ and are equal otherwise. The lower bound is the isolated-vertex threshold, and the authors note: ``we do not know how to prove that the cutoffs are exactly the same when $r \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$.''
rows.source_text: Do the cutoff for $\mathrm{FS}(X, Y)$ to avoid isolated vertices and the cutoff for $\mathrm{FS}(X, Y)$ to have exactly 2 connected components coincide when $r \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$? That is, is $d_{r,r} = \lceil (3r+1)/4 \rceil$ for all $r \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$?
rows.status_semantics: The conjecture asks whether $d_{r,r} = \lceil(3r+1)/4\rceil$ for all $r \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$, i.e., whether the cutoffs for $\mathrm{FS}(X,Y)$ to avoid isolated vertices and to have exactly two connected components coincide in this residue class. This was settled affirmatively by the paper arXiv:2309.03848 on bipartite friends-and-strangers graphs, whose Corollary 1.3 establishes $d_{r,r} = \lceil(3r+1)/4\rceil$ for all $r$ (including $r \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$), and explicitly states that this settles ADK Conjecture 7.4 (the journal-version numbering of the open question from arXiv:2009.07840). The same paper also proves, as a main theorem, that the two cutoffs are equal for all $r$.
rows.class_notes: Precise equality d_{r,r} = ceil((3r+1)/4), but d_{r,r} and the FS(X,Y) framework are not defined in this record's context; solved.

rows.paper_title: Fractional vertex-arboricity of planar graphs
rows.statement_text: Every planar graph has fractional vertex-arboricity at most two.
rows.context_text: This is the fractional generalization of the Albertson-Berman Conjecture: since $|V(G)|/a(G) \leq \mathrm{va}_f(G)$, the conjecture implies $a(G) \geq |V(G)|/2$. If true, it would also imply that every planar graph has fractional chromatic number at most four.

rows.title: Problem 1.2
rows.paper_title: Extension of Gyarfas-Sumner conjecture to digraphs
rows.statement_text: What are the finite sets $\mathcal{F}$ of digraphs for which the class $\mathrm{Forb}_{\mathrm{ind}}(\mathcal{F})$ has bounded dichromatic number?
rows.context_text: This is the central problem of the paper, extending the Gyárfás-Sumner interrogation to directed graphs via the dichromatic number $\vec{\chi}$. A finite set $\mathcal{F}$ of digraphs is called heroic if $\mathrm{Forb}_{\mathrm{ind}}(\mathcal{F})$ has bounded dichromatic number. The paper focuses primarily on characterizing heroic sets of size three.
rows.source_text: What are the finite sets $\mathcal{F}$ of digraphs for which the class $\mathrm{Forb}_{\mathrm{ind}}(\mathcal{F})$ has bounded dichromatic number?
rows.status_semantics: Problem 1.2 asks for a full characterization of all finite sets of digraphs that are heroic (i.e., whose avoidance guarantees bounded dichromatic number); this characterization remains open. Partial progress includes: locally out-transitive oriented graphs shown to have dichromatic number at most 2 (arXiv:2103.07886); (P6, triangle)-free oriented graphs shown to have dichromatic number at most 382 (arXiv:2212.02272); heroes in oriented complete multipartite graphs nearly fully characterized (arXiv:2202.13306). A 2026 preprint (arXiv:2602.08736) disproves the related conjecture that {oriented star forest, hero} always forms a heroic pair, by constructing (Claw, C3)-free orientations of rook graphs with unbounded dichromatic number.
rows.defer_reason: Grand-characterization request ('which / for which / characterize'), not a single proposition.

rows.title: Conjecture 4.2
rows.paper_title: Extension of Gyarfas-Sumner conjecture to digraphs
rows.statement_text: Let $H$ be a hero and let $F$ be an oriented forest. The set $\{\overleftrightarrow{K_2}, H, F\}$ is heroic if and only if: either $F$ is the disjoint union of oriented stars, or $H$ is a transitive tournament.
rows.context_text: This is the main conjecture of the paper, a digraph analog of the Gyárfás-Sumner conjecture for oriented graphs. The 'only if' direction is proved in Section 6.1. The case where both conditions hold simultaneously (H a transitive tournament and F a disjoint union of oriented stars) is already settled by Chudnovsky, Scott and Seymour [6].
rows.source_text: Let $H$ be a hero and let $F$ be an oriented forest. The set $\{\overleftrightarrow{K_2}, H, F\}$ is heroic if and only if: either $F$ is the disjoint union of oriented stars, or $H$ is a transitive tournament.

rows.status_semantics: The 'only if' direction of Conjecture 4.2 is established in the source paper, and the case where both conditions hold simultaneously was resolved prior to posting by Chudnovsky–Scott–Seymour. Several special cases of the 'if' direction have since been proved: Aboulker, Aubian, and Charbit (2021) prove the case F = S₂⁺ with H = C₃; Aboulker, Aubian, Charbit, and Thomassé (2022) establish bounded dichromatic number for ⃗P₆-free triangle-free oriented graphs. rows.title: Conjecture 4.4
rows.paper_title: Extension of Gyarfas-Sumner conjecture to digraphs
rows.statement_text: Given an oriented forest $F$ and for every integer $k$, $\{\overleftrightarrow{K_2}, K_k, F\}$ is heroic.

It generalises the heroic-set result for $\{\overleftrightarrow{K_2}, K_k, P^+(3)\}$ proved in Theorem 4.3, where $K_k$ denotes the digraph on $k$ vertices with no arc.

rows.status_semantics: Conjecture 4.4 — that $\{\overleftrightarrow{K_2}, K_k, F\}$ is heroic for every oriented forest $F$ and every integer $k$ — remains open in full generality. Two follow-up papers from the curated corpus establish special cases: arXiv:2103.07886 handles $F = S_2^+$ (oriented star with two out-edges) and arXiv:2212.02272 handles $F = \overrightarrow{P}_6$ with the clique constraint $\omega \le 2$ (triangle-free). rows.title: Near-sunflower analogue of the Erdős-Rado Sunflower Conjecture
rows.paper_title: Near-sunflowers and focal families
rows.statement_text: If $\mathcal{F}$ is a $k$-uniform family of sets containing no near-sunflower of size $r$, then $|\mathcal{F}| \leq C^k$, where $C$ is a constant depending only on $r$.
rows.context_text: The paper introduces near-sunflowers as a weakening of sunflowers (allowing elements to belong to $0, 1, r-1,$ or $r$ sets in the family) and proposes this bound as a weaker version of the notorious Erdős-Rado sunflower conjecture. While the paper resolves the Erdős-Szemerédi-type question (exponential bound in $n$) for near-sunflowers via Theorem 1.3, the Erdős-Rado-type question (exponential bound in $k$) is explicitly left open; Section 6 proves the bound only under a stronger condition.

rows.title: Conjecture 1.1

rows.statement_text: For $d \geq 1$ and $r \geq 3$, there is a constant $C = C(d, r)$ such that $f^d_r(k) \leq C^k$.
rows.context_text: The authors note that the Erdős-Rado sunflower conjecture implies this weaker statement about families of bounded VC-dimension $d$, where $f^d_r(k)$ is the minimum family size guaranteeing an $r$-sunflower among $k$-sets with VC-dimension at most $d$. The paper proves the conjecture for $d = 1$ (Theorem 1.2) and establishes the slightly weaker bound $f^d_r(k) \leq 2^{10k(dr)^2 \log^* k}$ for $d \geq 2$ (Theorem 1.3), leaving the full conjecture open for $d \geq 2$.

rows.status_semantics: The conjecture that $f^d_r(k) \leq C^k$ for all $d \geq 1$ and $r \geq 3$ is proven for $d=1$ by the original paper (Theorem 1.2). The $d=1$ case is also resolved sharply in 2408.04165 with the tight bound $(r-1)^k$.

rows.title: Open Problem: 5-Coloring complexity for H-free graphs with a P4 component
