rows.statement_text: The complexity of the $5$-Coloring Problem restricted to $H$-free graphs remains open when $H$ has exactly one connected component $C$ isomorphic to $P_4$, and $H - V(C)$ is an induced subgraph of $rP_3$ containing at least one edge for some $r \geq 1$.
rows.context_text: After proving that the $k$-Coloring Problem on $2P_4$-free graphs is NP-complete for all $k \geq 5$ (Theorem 7), the authors observe that combined with Theorem 4 this leaves the 5-Coloring complexity unresolved only for the described family of forbidden subgraphs $H$. This is the last remaining gap toward a full dichotomy for the $5$-Coloring Problem on $H$-free graphs.
rows.source_text: The complexity of the $5$-Coloring Problem restricted to $H$-free graphs remains open when $H$ has exactly one connected component $C$ isomorphic to $P_4$, and $H - V(C)$ is an induced subgraph of $rP_3$ containing at least one edge for some $r \geq 1$.
rows.source_locator: arXiv:2105.01787 — Open Problem: 5-Coloring complexity for H-free graphs with a P4 component
rows.status_semantics: The open problem about the complexity of the List-5-Coloring Problem restricted to H-free graphs, when H has a P4 component and H minus V(C) is an induced subgraph of rP3 containing at least one edge, was fully resolved by Chudnovsky, Hajebi, and Spirkl (arXiv:2311.05713, Combinatorica 2024). Their main theorem establishes a complete complexity dichotomy for List-k-Coloring on H-free graphs for all k > 4: the problem is polynomial-time solvable if and only if every component of H is a path on at most three vertices, or removing the isolated vertices of H leaves an induced subgraph of the five-vertex path P5. For every H in the conjecture's family, the non-isolated part of H contains a P4 plus at least one further edge (contributing at least 2 more vertices), giving at least 6 vertices total, which cannot embed in P5; since neither polynomial condition holds, List-5-Coloring is NP-complete for all such H-free graphs.

rows.status_semantics: The open question asks whether List-$k$-Coloring on $rP_3$-free graphs is NP-hard for some $k\in\mathbb{N}$. arXiv:2311.05713 (Chudnovsky, Hajebi, Spirkl; Combinatorica 2024) proves a full complexity dichotomy for all $k>4$: List-$k$-Coloring on $H$-free graphs is polynomial-time solvable whenever every component of $H$ is a path on at most three vertices, and $rP_3$ satisfies this condition. rows.title: Open problem on parameters governing $\overrightarrow{r}_1(H)$

The authors introduce the notion of 'multiscale complexity' as a candidate parameter for the directed setting, but stress that the full picture remains unresolved and deserves further research.

rows.status_semantics: The source paper itself already demonstrates that bounded degree alone does not suffice for polynomial (let alone linear) oriented Ramsey numbers, constructing bounded-degree acyclic digraphs with $\overrightarrow{r}_1(H) \ge n^{\Omega(\Delta^{2/3}/\log^{5/3}\Delta)}$, while the complete characterization via natural parameters remains open. The 2025 follow-up by Bradač, Morawski, Sudakov, and Wigderson extends the linear upper bound regime to acyclic digraphs with 'graded bandwidth' (local edge structure), unifying previous results on bounded height, bounded bandwidth, and tree blowups. However, the full picture is explicitly acknowledged as far from resolved: a complete analogue of the degeneracy-plus-vertex-count framework for undirected graphs has not been found for the directed setting.

rows.title: Question 1
rows.paper_title: Geometric and o-minimal Littlewood-Offord problems
rows.statement_text: Assuming only that each $a_i \neq 0$, what geometric constraints can be imposed on a set $S \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ which imply non-trivial uniform upper bounds on $\Pr(X \in S)$?
rows.context_text: The paper introduces a new generalisation of the Littlewood–Offord problem to $\mathbb{R}^d$ in which no assumption is made on the sizes of the nonzero vectors $a_1,\ldots,a_n$, only that they are nonzero. The authors observe that this makes the question much more about the geometry of $S$ than about spatial anti-concentration of $X = a_1\xi_1 + \cdots + a_n\xi_n$, giving it a very different flavour from previous Littlewood–Offord variants.
rows.source_text: Assuming only that each $a_i \neq 0$, what geometric constraints can be imposed on a set $S \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ which imply non-trivial uniform upper bounds on $\Pr(X \in S)$?
rows.status_semantics: Question 1 from arXiv:2106.04894 asks, for arbitrary nonzero vectors $a_i$, which geometric constraints on $S \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ yield non-trivial uniform upper bounds on $\Pr(X \in S)$. The source paper itself answers this for o-minimal sets (those definable in an o-minimal structure) not containing a line segment, giving a bound of $n^{-1/2+o(1)}$. A 2025 paper by Grebennikov and Kwan (arXiv:2505.24699) extends this programme substantially, proving that sets in convex position and algebraic varieties of prescribed dimension and degree also yield such bounds, thereby resolving Conjecture 10.1 of Fox-Kwan-Spink as well as a conjecture of Kwan-Sauermann; the general question of characterising all admissible geometric constraints remains an open research direction.
rows.defer_reason: Littlewood-Offord anti-concentration in R^d: probability/geometry, not graph theory; also a vague what-question

rows.title: Conjecture 1.2
rows.paper_title: Geometric and o-minimal Littlewood-Offord problems
rows.statement_text: In Theorem 1.1 we have $\Pr(X \in S) \leq C_S/\sqrt{n}$, for some $C_S$ depending only on $S$.
rows.context_text: Theorem 1.1 establishes $\Pr(X \in S) \leq n^{-1/2+\alpha}$ for any $\alpha > 0$ when $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ is definable with respect to an o-minimal structure and contains no line segment; the conjecture posits that the optimal $O(1/\sqrt{n})$ bound from the classical Erd\H{o}s–Littlewood–Offord theorem also holds in this geometric setting. The authors prove it when $S$ satisfies the generic intersection property, which covers convex or irreducible algebraic plane curves in $\mathbb{R}^2$, irreducible complex algebraic curves, and the boundary of a 3-dimensional ball. They also remark that a full resolution of the Gotsman–Linial conjecture would imply Conjecture 1.2 for all semi-algebraic sets not containing a line segment.
rows.source_text: In Theorem 1.1 we have $\Pr(X \in S) \leq C_S/\sqrt{n}$, for some $C_S$ depending only on $S$.
rows.status_semantics: Conjecture 1.2 — the optimal $O(1/\sqrt{n})$ anti-concentration bound for random signed sums landing in an o-minimal set containing no line segment — has been established for the semialgebraic case by Grebennikov and Kwan (2025, arXiv:2505.24699), who prove $\Pr[\xi_1 a_1+\cdots+\xi_n a_n \in S] \le O_S(n^{-1/2})$ via a lattice-point-counting reduction; the paper explicitly states it resolves conjectures of Fox–Kwan–Spink and Kwan–Sauermann. Whether this covers the full conjecture for all o-minimal (not just semialgebraic) structures is not confirmed from the available abstract and HTML.

rows.status_semantics: The remark in arXiv:2107.11780 that star-forests, double stars, K₂, and their induced subgraphs might constitute the complete list of forests H for which H-free graphs are polynomially χ-bounded is refuted: Nguyen (December 2025, arXiv:2512.24907) proved that P₅-free graphs are polynomially χ-bounded, and P₅ is a forest that is not an induced subgraph of any star, double star, or K₂. Separately, Briański–Davies–Walczak (2022, arXiv:2201.08814) disproved Esperet’s general conjecture by constructing hereditary χ-bounded classes that are not polynomially χ-bounded, confirming that polynomial χ-bounds are not automatic even within χ-bounded classes.

rows.title: Conjecture 1.1
rows.paper_title: Irregular Subgraphs
rows.statement_text: Every $d$-regular graph $G$ on $n$ vertices contains a spanning subgraph $H$ so that for every $k$, $0 \leq k \leq d$, $\left|m(H, k) - \frac{n}{d+1}\right| \leq 2$.
rows.context_text: The paper introduces this conjecture as one of two central open problems on irregular spanning subgraphs. A small value of $m(H)$ measures the irregularity of $H$, and the conjecture asserts that every $d$-regular graph has a spanning subgraph nearly as irregular as its degree permits. The conjecture is tight: the vertex-disjoint union of two 4-cycles shows the additive 2 cannot be reduced to 1 in general.

rows.status_semantics: Conjecture 1.1 remains open for general d, but significant partial progress has been made. Ma and Xie (2024) proved, via deterministic local adjustment techniques, that the conjecture holds exactly for d=3 (cubic graphs, in a strong form) and gave a general bound |m(H,k) - n/(d+1)| ≤ 2d² independent of n for all d-regular graphs — the first such n-independent bound.

rows.title: Conjecture 1.2
rows.paper_title: Irregular Subgraphs
rows.statement_text: Every graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and minimum degree $\delta$ contains a spanning subgraph $H$ satisfying $m(H) \leq \frac{n}{\delta+1} + 2$.
rows.context_text: This is the second of the two central conjectures introduced by the authors, generalising Conjecture 1.1 from regular graphs to arbitrary graphs with minimum degree $\delta$. Both conjectures remain open; the paper proves asymptotic relaxations showing the bound $(1+o(1))\frac{n}{\delta+1}+2$ is achievable when $n$ is large.

rows.status_semantics: Conjecture 1.2 from arXiv:2108.02685 remains open in full generality. Fox, Luo, and Pham (2022) proved the asymptotic version for d-regular graphs when d = o(n/(log n)^{12}) via probabilistic methods. rows.title: Conjecture 7
rows.paper_title: Improved pyrotechnics : Closer to the burning graph conjecture
rows.statement_text: Let $T$ be a tree of growth $k$ and of order $n$. If $R$ is a finite set of integers such that $\{0, 1, \ldots, k\} \subseteq R$ and $\sum_{r \in R}(2r+1) \geq n$, then $T$ is $R$-burnable.
rows.context_text: The authors propose this as a stronger version of the Burning Number Conjecture via a reformulation using $R$-burnability: the BNC states that every connected graph on $n$ vertices is $\{0, 1, \ldots, \lceil\sqrt{n}\rceil - 1\}$-burnable, since $\sum_{r=0}^{\lceil\sqrt{n}\rceil - 1}(2r+1) = \lceil\sqrt{n}\rceil^2 \geq n$. Conjecture 7 generalises this to trees of bounded growth by requiring the set $R$ to contain all radii up to $k$ and have sufficient total volume.

rows.paper_title: Active clustering for labeling training data
rows.statement_text: For an $n$-set with a random partition with probabilities $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_k$, the clique algorithm has minimal average complexity among all AC algorithms.
rows.context_text: In the model where each of $n$ items independently belongs to class $C_i$ with probability $p_i$ (with $p_1 \geq p_2 \geq \cdots \geq p_k$), the authors argue that an optimal algorithm should compare each new element first to the largest identified class. The clique algorithm does exactly this, comparing each new item to blocks in decreasing order of size. The conjecture is stated directly before Theorem 6, which characterises the asymptotic expected query count of the clique algorithm as $\sum_{i=1}^k i p_i n$, offered as supporting evidence.

rows.title: Conjecture (Section 7)
rows.paper_title: Discrepancy of arithmetic progressions in grids
rows.statement_text: The lower bound for the discrepancy of arithmetic progressions in grids given in Theorem 1.3 is tight up to the constant factor, i.e., for any positive integer $d$ and $N = (N_1, \ldots, N_d)$ with $N_1 \cdots N_d \geq 3$, $$\mathrm{disc}(\mathcal{A}_N) = \Theta_d\!\left(\max_{I \subseteq [d]} \left(\prod_{i \in I} N_i\right)^{\frac{1}{2|I|+2}}\right).$$
rows.context_text: Theorem 1.3 establishes matching lower and upper bounds for the discrepancy of arithmetic progressions in general grids of differing side lengths, but the upper bound carries an extra sub-logarithmic factor $\frac{\log(N_1 \cdots N_d)}{\log\log(N_1 \cdots N_d)}$ relative to the lower bound. The authors conjecture in their concluding remarks (Section 7) that this gap is an artifact of the proof and the lower bound is in fact tight up to a constant depending only on $d$.
rows.source_text: The lower bound for the discrepancy of arithmetic progressions in grids given in Theorem 1.3 is tight up to the constant factor, i.e., for any positive integer $d$ and $N = (N_1, \ldots, N_d)$ with $N_1 \cdots N_d \geq 3$, $$\mathrm{disc}(\mathcal{A}_N) = \Theta_d\!\left(\max_{I \subseteq [d]} \left(\prod_{i \in I} N_i\right)^{\frac{1}{2|I|+2}}\right).$$
rows.status_semantics: The conjecture that the lower bound in Theorem 1.3 is tight up to a constant factor (i.e., no logarithmic factor) remains open. Li and Nikolov (2025, arXiv:2504.12598) improved the upper bound gap from a factor of log|Omega_N|/(log log|Omega_N|) to sqrt(log|Omega_N|), using factorization norms, but explicitly state that removing this final sqrt(log) factor is beyond their methods. The conjecture itself is restated as open in that paper.

rows.status_semantics: The open challenge of efficiently approximating twin-width for unordered graphs remains unresolved for general graphs, as confirmed by Bonnet's own open-questions page (updated 2025). Partial progress exists: an FPT approximation algorithm has been found for graphs with small feedback edge number (Balabán, Ganian, Rocton 2023), but no XP or FPT approximation is known for the general unordered case. Exact computation of twin-width is NP-hard—deciding whether twin-width is at most 4 is NP-complete.

rows.title: Question 1.3
rows.paper_title: Pure pairs. IX. Transversal trees
rows.statement_text: Do there exist $c, \varepsilon > 0$ with the following property? Let $\mathcal{B} = (B_1, B_2, B_3)$ be a blockade in a graph $G$, and let $W$ be its width. If there is no $\mathcal{B}$-transversal triangle, then there exist distinct $i, j \in \{1, 2, 3\}$ and $X \subseteq B_i$ and $Y \subseteq B_j$, such that $X, Y$ is a pure pair, and $|X|, |Y| \geq \varepsilon W^c$.
rows.context_text: This is a variant of a conjecture of Conlon, Fox and Sudakov. Settling Question 1.3 was the authors' initial goal, though they were unable to do so. It is also equivalent to the $k=3$ case of Theorem 1.4 (which handles cycles of length $k \geq 4$), and can be reduced to the sparse case where every vertex in $B_i$ has at most $|B_j|/100$ neighbours in $B_j$ for all distinct $i, j \in \{1,2,3\}$.

rows.title: Polynomial Kempe sequences for degenerate graphs
rows.paper_title: Kempe changes in degenerate graphs
rows.statement_text: Can any two $k$-colorings of a $(k-1)$-degenerate graph on $n$ vertices always be connected by a sequence of Kempe changes whose length is polynomial in $n$?
rows.context_text: Las Vergnas and Meyniel proved in 1981 that all $k$-colorings of a $d$-degenerate graph are Kempe equivalent when $k > d+1$, but their proof yields a sequence that may be exponential in the number of vertices. Whether a polynomial bound can be achieved is posed as an intriguing open question and is the central motivation for all three main results of the paper.

rows.statement_text: Fix an integer $r \geq 4$. Is it true that every $K_r$-free segment graph on $n$ vertices has an induced subgraph on $\Omega_r(n)$ vertices which is $K_{r-1}$-free?
rows.context_text: Motivated by the approach of coloring $K_r$-free string graphs to prove Conjecture 1.1: if each color class could be made $K_4$-free, Ackerman's result would bound the edges per class by $O(n)$. Although Krawczyk–Walczak showed $K_r$-free string graphs can require $\Omega_r(\log\log n)$ colors with $K_{r-1}$-free classes, the question of finding a linearly large $K_{r-1}$-free induced subgraph in a $K_r$-free segment graph remains open. The paper's Theorems 1.5 and 1.6 address analogous questions for string graphs (with a $\log^2 n$ loss), but the segment-graph case with a linear guarantee is unresolved.

rows.title: Conjecture 1.3
rows.paper_title: Polynomial bounds for chromatic number. V. Excluding a tree of radius two and a complete multipartite graph
rows.statement_text: For every forest $H$, there is a polynomial $f$ such that $\chi(G) \leq f(\omega(G))$ for every $H$-free graph $G$.
rows.context_text: This conjecture is presented as what the Gyárfás-Sumner conjecture (1.1) and Esperet's conjecture (that every $\chi$-bounded hereditary class has a polynomial bounding function) would jointly imply for forest-free graph classes. Esperet's conjecture has been disproved in full generality but remains open for classes excluding a forest, and Conjecture 1.3 is known only for a few special families of trees.

rows.status_semantics: Conjecture 1.3 — polynomial chi-boundedness for every forest-free graph class — remains open in full generality as of May 2026. Significant partial progress has been made: Nguyen (arXiv:2512.24907, 2025) proved the conjecture for H = P_5, the five-vertex path, resolving a case open since 1985; Davies and Yuditsky (arXiv:2407.16882, 2024) proved it for all forests H when the host graphs have bounded boxicity. The ongoing Scott–Seymour series establishes polynomial bounds for several additional tree families, but no uniform proof for all forests exists.

rows.statement_text: Is it possible to decrease the bound to $n$ in Theorem 2 (or at least in Theorem 1)?
rows.context_text: The paper proves that intersection graphs of $f$-space-filling systems of subsets of a metric space of Assouad-Nagata dimension $n$ have asymptotic dimension at most $2n+1$. rows.title: Open problem (disjoint union of good trees)
rows.paper_title: Polynomial bounds for chromatic number VII. Disjoint holes
rows.statement_text: It is not known that if trees $H_1$, $H_2$ are good (i.e., the class of $H_i$-free graphs is polynomially $\chi$-bounded for $i=1,2$), then the disjoint union of $H_1$ and $H_2$ is also good.
rows.context_text: Trees of diameter three are good [14], but whether disjoint unions of diameter-three trees are good is unknown. Self-isolation provides a sufficient condition: if $H_1$ and $H_2$ are good forests and one of them is self-isolating, their disjoint union is good.
rows.source_text: It is not known that if trees $H_1$, $H_2$ are good (i.e., the class of $H_i$-free graphs is polynomially $\chi$-bounded for $i=1,2$), then the disjoint union of $H_1$ and $H_2$ is also good.
rows.source_locator: arXiv:2202.09118 — Open problem (disjoint union of good trees) | Rocq: chromatic-theory/theories/conjectures/X66.v#good_trees_disjoint_union_good_statement
rows.verification_note: Authored in X66.v:good_trees_disjoint_union_good_statement. Encodes the open problem that the disjoint union of two good trees is good.
rows.status_semantics: The general question of whether the disjoint union of two good trees is always good remains open as of 2026. Partial progress exists: arXiv:2202.10412 (submitted three days after the source paper) proves that if $H$ is a good forest then $H \cup P_4$ is also good, and the source paper itself notes that the disjoint union of two good forests is good whenever one is self-isolating. No paper resolving the full conjecture was found in the indexed literature.
rows.class_notes: 'Good' is defined inline (poly chi-bounded H-free class), so the closure-under-disjoint-union statement is self-contained.

rows.title: Question (are all graphs self-isolating?)
rows.paper_title: Polynomial bounds for chromatic number VII. Disjoint holes
rows.statement_text: Could it be that all graphs are self-isolating?
rows.context_text: The authors note that they know very few graphs that have the self-isolating property and none that are known not to have it. The only connected graphs known to be self-isolating are complete graphs, paths of arbitrary length, and complete bipartite graphs (proved in the paper and its predecessors).
rows.source_text: Could it be that all graphs are self-isolating?
rows.class_notes: 'Self-isolating' is paper-local and not defined in the record.

rows.title: Informal Conjecture (every forest is good)
rows.paper_title: Polynomial bounds for chromatic number VI. Adding a four-vertex path
rows.statement_text: Perhaps every forest is good (i.e., for every forest $H$, the class of $H$-free graphs is polynomially $\chi$-bounded).
rows.context_text: After recalling that Esperet's conjecture that every $\chi$-bounded hereditary class is polynomially $\chi$-bounded was disproved, the authors ask which hereditary classes are polynomially $\chi$-bounded and raise in particular whether the Gyárfás-Sumner conjecture can be strengthened to polynomial $\chi$-boundedness. They note that among trees, only those not containing $P_5$ are currently known to be good, and that it is not even known whether $P_5$ is good.
rows.source_text: Perhaps every forest is good (i.e., for every forest $H$, the class of $H$-free graphs is polynomially $\chi$-bounded).
rows.source_locator: arXiv:2202.10412 — Informal Conjecture (every forest is good) | Rocq: chromatic-theory/theories/conjectures/X218.v#every_forest_is_good_statement
rows.verification_note: Authored in X218.v:every_forest_is_good_statement. Chudnovsky-Scott-Seymour-Spirkl: every forest H is 'good', i.e. the H-free class is polynomially chi-bounded, in the shared normal form chi <= c * omega^d (Chromatic.foundations chi_bounding.poly_chi_bounded). Same mathematical conjecture as arxiv:2202.05557#00 (X65.v), which encodes the polynomial as a coefficient list. implications_X218.v proves it implies the multibounding row (corpus edge e171, status=verified).
rows.status_semantics: The conjecture that every forest H is good (H-free graphs are polynomially χ-bounded) remains open in general, but has seen major progress. At the time of the source paper, P₅ was the smallest forest not known to be good; in December 2025 Tung H. Nguyen (arXiv:2512.24907) proved that P₅-free graphs are polynomially χ-bounded, resolving that open case. The polynomial Gyárfás-Sumner conjecture has also been established for bounded-boxicity graphs (arXiv:2407.16882). Forests requiring longer induced paths (P₆ and beyond) remain open.
rows.class_notes: Chudnovsky-Scott-Seymour-Spirkl informal conjecture: every forest H is 'good', i.e. the class of H-free graphs is polynomially chi-bounded. Modelling: 'polynomially chi-bounded' is exists c d, forall G H-free, chi(G) <= c * omega(G)^d.

rows.title: Conjecture 2.3
rows.paper_title: Polynomial bounds for chromatic number VI. Adding a four-vertex path
rows.statement_text: Let $\psi, \sigma : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be non-decreasing polynomials, let $q \geq 0$ an integer, and let $H$ be a broom. Then there is a non-decreasing polynomial $\phi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that if $G$ is a graph, and $\chi(G) > \phi(\omega(G))$, and $G$ contains no $(\psi, q)$-scattering, then $G$ [contains] a $\sigma$-nondominating copy of $H$.
rows.context_text: The authors remark that Conjecture 2.3 is 'an appealing possible strengthening of 2.2 that we could not prove.' Theorem 2.2 (which is proved) requires $H$ to be a broom and $J$ a path, finding both; Conjecture 2.3 would give a $\sigma$-nondominating copy of a broom alone without needing a path. This would extend the self-isolating property (proved for paths as Corollary 2.4) to brooms.
rows.source_text: Let $\psi, \sigma : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be non-decreasing polynomials, let $q \geq 0$ an integer, and let $H$ be a broom. Then there is a non-decreasing polynomial $\phi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that if $G$ is a graph, and $\chi(G) > \phi(\omega(G))$, and $G$ contains no $(\psi, q)$-scattering, then $G$ [contains] a $\sigma$-nondominating copy of $H$.
rows.class_notes: Technical strengthening toward polynomial Gyarfas-Sumner; (psi,q)-scattering and sigma-nondominating are paper-local.

rows.title: Conjecture 3
rows.paper_title: Exact Matching in Graphs of Bounded Independence Number
rows.statement_text: The problem of counting perfect matchings in input graphs of independence number $2$ is $\#P$-complete.
rows.context_text: The authors note that for all previously known graph classes on which EM is tractable (planar graphs, $K_{3,3}$-minor-free graphs, complete and complete bipartite graphs), counting perfect matchings is also polynomial. Their new results for graphs of independence number 2 break this alignment, since no polynomial counting scheme is known for this class and the authors believe counting is hard.
rows.source_text: The problem of counting perfect matchings in input graphs of independence number $2$ is $\#P$-complete.
rows.status_semantics: Conjecture 3 from arXiv:2202.11988, asserting that counting perfect matchings in graphs of independence number at most 2 is #P-complete, was resolved by El Maalouly and Wang in arXiv:2210.15014 (October 2022). Their paper proves #P-completeness for both general graphs with independence number ≤ 2 and bipartite graphs with bipartite independence number ≤ 2, via reductions from counting perfect matchings in bipartite graphs using graph-theoretic constructions.
rows.class_notes: #P-completeness of counting perfect matchings at independence number 2; solved, needs complexity foundation.

rows.title: Question 1.4
rows.paper_title: Heroes in oriented complete multipartite graphs
rows.statement_text: Is $\Delta(1,2,2)$ a hero in oriented complete multipartite graphs?
rows.context_text: The paper characterizes heroes in oriented complete multipartite graphs up to the status of $\Delta(1,2,2)$. If the answer is no, heroes in oriented complete multipartite graphs are precisely those described in Theorem 1.3; if the answer is yes, a different complete characterization involving $\Delta(1,2,2)$ holds.
rows.source_text: Is $\Delta(1,2,2)$ a hero in oriented complete multipartite graphs?
rows.verification_note: Authored in X221.v:delta122_hero_oriented_complete_multipartite_statement. Question 1.4: is Delta(1,2,2) a hero in oriented complete multipartite graphs? dichromatic_bounded of the class of x221_oriented_complete_multipartite (oriented + transitive non-adjacency) Delta(1,2,2)-free digraphs. The corpus row is DISPROVED (Walczak, Remark 1.5 of the published version), so the Prop is expected false; no refutation is committed.
rows.status_semantics: Question 1.4 is answered negatively: Δ(1,2,2) is not a hero in oriented complete multipartite graphs. Remark 1.5 of the revised paper (v2, December 2023; published Journal of Graph Theory 105(4):652–669, 2024) records that Bartosz Walczak proved non-interlaced ordered graphs have unbounded chromatic number, which together with Theorem 4.2 of the paper implies Δ(1,2,2) is not a hero. Consequently, heroes in oriented complete multipartite graphs are precisely those characterised in Theorem 1.3.
rows.class_notes: Aboulker-Aubian-Charbit Question 1.4: is Delta(1,2,2) a hero in oriented complete multipartite graphs?

rows.title: Question 5.4
rows.paper_title: Heroes in oriented complete multipartite graphs
rows.statement_text: Let $H$ and $F$ be digraphs such that $\Delta(1,1,H)$ is a hero in $Forb_{ind}(F)$ and $H$ is a hero in $Forb_{ind}(K_{1}+F)$. Then $\Delta(1,1,H)$ is a hero in $Forb_{ind}(K_{1}+F)$.
rows.context_text: This question asks whether a compositional hero property transfers across the $K_1 + F$ operation. It is motivated by the observation that knowing heroes in $Forb_{ind}(\bar{K}_t)$ does not straightforwardly help in understanding heroes in $Forb_{ind}(\bar{K}_{t+1})$, even though such a transfer would be natural.
rows.source_text: Let $H$ and $F$ be digraphs such that $\Delta(1,1,H)$ is a hero in $Forb_{ind}(F)$ and $H$ is a hero in $Forb_{ind}(K_{1}+F)$. Then $\Delta(1,1,H)$ is a hero in $Forb_{ind}(K_{1}+F)$.
rows.class_notes: Compositional hero transfer across K_1+F; hero/Forb_ind/join vocabulary standard in this literature though the join convention for digraphs needs fixing carefully.

rows.title: Conjecture 1.5
rows.paper_title: Pure pairs. X. Tournaments and the strong Erdos-Hajnal property
rows.statement_text: A tournament has the strong EH-property if and only if it admits a numbering for which the backedge graph is a forest.
rows.context_text: The paper proves (Theorem 1.4) that the forward direction holds: every tournament with the strong EH-property admits a numbering for which the backedge graph is a forest. The authors initially thought the converse unlikely but failed to find a counterexample. This would be a tournament analogue of Theorem 1.3, which characterises graphs with the strong EH-property as those for which one of $H$ or $\bar{H}$ is a forest.
rows.source_text: A tournament has the strong EH-property if and only if it admits a numbering for which the backedge graph is a forest.
rows.class_notes: Needs strong-EH-property primitive (linear pure pairs in tournaments) plus backedge-graph-of-numbering definition; both buildable.

rows.title: Informal question: can the D5-freeness hypothesis in Theorem 1.6 be dropped?
rows.paper_title: Pure pairs. X. Tournaments and the strong Erdos-Hajnal property
rows.statement_text: Perhaps the second sentence in 1.6 (the condition that $H$ is $D_5$-free) can be omitted, but that remains open.
rows.context_text: Theorem 1.6 states that if a tournament $H$ admits a numbering $(v_1,\ldots,v_n)$ whose backedge graph $B$ has at most three edges, and $H$ is $D_5$-free, then $H$ has the strong EH-property. The $D_5$-freeness condition excludes exactly the case where the three backedges form the unique three-edge backedge graph of $D_5$; the authors leave open whether this exclusion is truly necessary.
rows.source_text: Perhaps the second sentence in 1.6 (the condition that $H$ is $D_5$-free) can be omitted, but that remains open.
rows.source_locator: arXiv:2202.13977 — Informal question: can the D5-freeness hypothesis in Theorem 1.6 be dropped?
rows.class_notes: Context fully reconstructs the proposition: every tournament with a numbering whose backedge graph has at most 3 edges has the strong EH-property (D5-freeness dropped).

rows.title: Girth Conjecture (strengthening of Theorem 3)
rows.paper_title: Induced subgraphs of induced subgraphs of large chromatic number
rows.statement_text: For every triangle-free graph $F$, there is a constant $c_F$ and graphs $G$ of arbitrarily large chromatic number and the same girth as $F$ such that every $F$-free induced subgraph of $G$ is $c_F$-colourable.
rows.context_text: Theorem 3 guarantees, for triangle-free $F$, a triangle-free $G$, but does not control the girth of $G$. The authors ask whether $G$ can be taken to have the same girth as $F$, conjecture that this is so, but are unable to prove it. As a partial result they prove Theorem 4, the weaker analogue where girth is replaced by odd girth.
rows.source_text: For every triangle-free graph $F$, there is a constant $c_F$ and graphs $G$ of arbitrarily large chromatic number and the same girth as $F$ such that every $F$-free induced subgraph of $G$ is $c_F$-colourable.
rows.source_locator: arXiv:2203.03612 — Girth Conjecture (strengthening of Theorem 3) | Rocq: chromatic-theory/theories/conjectures/X50.v#triangle_free_same_girth_high_chromatic_induced_free_statement
rows.verification_note: Authored in X50.v:triangle_free_same_girth_high_chromatic_induced_free_statement. Encodes the same-girth triangle-free row: for each triangle-free F there are arbitrarily high-chromatic graphs with the same girth and bounded-chromatic F-free induced subgraphs.
rows.class_notes: Standard vocabulary throughout (girth, chromatic number, F-free induced subgraphs); ∀F ∃c_F ∀k ∃G shape.

rows.title: Conjecture 1.6
rows.paper_title: Induced subgraphs and tree decompositions IV. (Even hole, diamond, pyramid)-free graphs
rows.statement_text: For all $t > 0$ there exists $c_t \geq 0$ such that $\mathrm{tw}(G) \leq c_t$ for every $G \in \mathcal{C}^*_t$.
rows.context_text: Here $\mathcal{C}^*_t$ denotes the class of $(C_4, \text{diamond}, \text{theta}, \text{prism}, \text{even wheel}, K_t)$-free graphs — a relaxation of $\mathcal{C}_t$ in which pyramids are no longer excluded. The authors pose this as a slight generalization of Sintiari–Trotignon's Conjecture 1.5, noting that Theorem 1.4 (the main result of the paper) would serve as the base case if the conjecture could be proved by the same techniques.
rows.source_text: For all $t > 0$ there exists $c_t \geq 0$ such that $\mathrm{tw}(G) \leq c_t$ for every $G \in \mathcal{C}^*_t$.
rows.verification_note: Authored in X220.v:theta_prism_even_wheel_free_bounded_treewidth_statement. Abrishami-Chudnovsky-Hajebi-Spirkl Conjecture 1.6: for every t the class C*_t of (C_4, diamond, theta, prism, even wheel, K_t)-free graphs has bounded treewidth. Modelling of the three-path configurations: a THETA is a subdivision of K_2,3 (x220_theta), a PRISM is a subdivision of the 3-prism in which the six triangle edges are left unsubdivided (x220_prism), both via the subdiv_model record; an EVEN WHEEL is a hole plus an outside vertex with at least three neighbours on it, x220_even_wheel_free saying every such whee
rows.class_notes: Abrishami-Chudnovsky-Hajebi-Spirkl Conjecture 1.6: for every t the class of (C_4, diamond, theta, prism, even wheel, K_t)-free graphs has bounded treewidth.

rows.title: Open Question (unit segment graphs delineation)
rows.paper_title: Twin-width VIII: delineation and win-wins
rows.statement_text: Are unit segment graphs delineated (by twin-width)?
rows.context_text: The paper establishes that axis-parallel $H_t$-free unit segment graphs have bounded twin-width, while axis-parallel $H_4$-free two-lengthed segment graphs have unbounded twin-width, and that (triangle-free) pure axis-parallel unit segment graphs have unbounded twin-width. This places unit segment graphs at the frontier between delineated and non-delineated intersection graph classes, and the authors explicitly leave their delineation status as an open question.
rows.source_text: Are unit segment graphs delineated (by twin-width)?
rows.source_locator: arXiv:2204.00722 — Open Question (unit segment graphs delineation)
rows.status_semantics: The open question of whether unit segment graphs are delineated (by twin-width) remains unresolved for the general class, but significant partial progress has been made. Geniet, Kim, and Meijer (arXiv:2512.21896, 2025) prove that delineation holds for intersection graphs of non-degenerate axis-parallel unit segment graphs, while also showing that delineation fails for visibility graphs of 1.5D terrains; additionally the paper's body discusses non-delineation for more general unit segment variants (degenerate axis-parallel and arbitrary-slope unit segments). The non-degenerate axis-parallel subcase is thus settled positively, but the status of the full class of unit segment graphs — as posed in arXiv:2204.00722 — remains unresolved or at best partially answered negatively for broader subclasses.
rows.class_notes: 'Delineated' is a paper-defined notion (Twin-width VIII) not defined in the record; also needs geometric unit-segment-graph layer.

rows.title: Conjecture on r-free digraphs with r > 2n/3
rows.paper_title: Extremal results on feedback arc sets in digraphs
rows.statement_text: All $r$-free digraphs on $n$ vertices with $r > 2n/3$ are at most one edge away from being acyclic.
rows.context_text: The authors first construct a family of $r$-free digraphs $G$ on $n$ vertices with $\beta(G) \geq n^2/(r+1)^2$, implying that if every $r$-free digraph satisfies $\beta(G) = O(1)$ then $r = \Omega(n)$. In the converse direction they pose this conjecture, noting tightness: for $n$ a multiple of $3$ there exists an $(r-1)$-free digraph $G$ on $n$ vertices with $r = 2n/3$ and $\beta(G) = 2$.
rows.source_text: All $r$-free digraphs on $n$ vertices with $r > 2n/3$ are at most one edge away from being acyclic.
rows.source_locator: arXiv:2204.01938 — Conjecture on r-free digraphs with r > 2n/3
rows.status_semantics: A January 2026 MIT PRIMES research paper by Kai Lum (mentored by Nitya Mani, one of the conjecture's authors) proves that β(G) ≤ 1 for all r-free digraphs on n vertices with r > ⌊2n/3⌋, directly resolving the conjecture. The source paper (arXiv:2204.01938) was subsequently published in Random Structures & Algorithms (2024). No peer-reviewed journal or arXiv paper proving this conjecture was found; the only identified proof is in an unreviewed PRIMES preprint whose PDF could not be fully read, hence medium confidence.
rows.class_notes: 'r-free digraph' is paper-local and not defined in context; once recovered (no directed cycle of length <= r) the statement beta(G)<=1 is clean. Solved.

rows.title: Suspected directed surplus of a random B-free orientation (Remark 1.6)
rows.paper_title: Extremal results on feedback arc sets in digraphs

rows.title: Informal Conjecture (uniform twin-width strictly stronger than twin-width)
rows.paper_title: Twin-width VII: groups
rows.statement_text: Uniform twin-width is strictly stronger than twin-width, i.e. there are groups with finite twin-width and infinite uniform twin-width.
rows.context_text: Uniform twin-width requires a uniform bound on the permutation width of the action of every group element, whereas finite twin-width only requires each action to have finite width individually. Having finite uniform twin-width implies finite twin-width, but the converse is not established. The group of finitely supported permutations on $\mathbb{Z}$ is proposed as a candidate counterexample.
rows.source_text: Uniform twin-width is strictly stronger than twin-width, i.e. there are groups with finite twin-width and infinite uniform twin-width.
rows.source_locator: arXiv:2204.12330 — Informal Conjecture (uniform twin-width strictly stronger than twin-width)
rows.class_notes: Twin-width and uniform twin-width of infinite groups; 'permutation width of the action' is paper-local and not fully defined in the record.

rows.title: Question (explicit group with infinite twin-width)
rows.paper_title: Twin-width VII: groups
rows.statement_text: Can we find a more explicit construction of a group with infinite twin-width, or one with a direct proof that twin-width is infinite?
rows.context_text: The group constructed in Theorem 1.1 relies on probabilistic methods and starts from a sequence of bounded degree graphs with unbounded twin-width; it does not yield an explicit bounded degree graph with unbounded twin-width. A more explicit or combinatorially direct construction would significantly advance understanding of twin-width for bounded degree graphs.

rows.title: Open Problem (separating twin-width and queue number on sparse graphs)
rows.paper_title: Twin-width VII: groups
rows.statement_text: Separating twin-width and queue number on sparse graphs is an open problem.
rows.context_text: Finite queue number implies finite twin-width, so the two parameters are not equivalent in general. However, no example of a group (or sparse graph) with finite twin-width and infinite queue number is known, and the same gap exists for the corresponding uniform variants. Many results of the paper hold simultaneously for both parameters, making a separation elusive.

rows.title: Conjecture 1.6
rows.paper_title: 11/4-colorability of subcubic triangle-free graphs
rows.statement_text: Every subcubic triangle-free graph avoiding $F^{(1)}_{14}$, $F^{(2)}_{14}$, $F_{11}$, and $F_{22}$ as subgraphs is fractionally $19/7$-colorable.
rows.context_text: The authors pose this as an intermediate conjecture between their main result (Theorem 1.4, giving $11/4$-colorability when only $F^{(1)}_{14}$ and $F^{(2)}_{14}$ are excluded) and Conjecture 1.3 (giving $8/3$-colorability when six graphs are excluded). It is noted that $F_{11}$ and $F_{22}$ both have fractional chromatic number exactly $11/4$, while $F^{(1)}_{19}$ and $F^{(2)}_{19}$ have fractional chromatic number $19/7$, motivating this intermediate bound.
rows.source_text: Every subcubic triangle-free graph avoiding $F^{(1)}_{14}$, $F^{(2)}_{14}$, $F_{11}$, and $F_{22}$ as subgraphs is fractionally $19/7$-colorable.
rows.class_notes: The forbidden graphs F14^(1), F14^(2), F11, F22 are paper-specific named graphs not defined in the record; fractional 19/7-colorability itself is bounded/rational.

rows.title: Problem 1.6
rows.paper_title: On density of $Z_3$-flow-critical graphs
rows.statement_text: What is the smallest constant $\alpha$ such that every $Z_3$-flow-critical graph $G$ satisfies $|E(G)| \leq \frac{5}{2}|V(G)| + \alpha g(G) + O(1)$?
rows.context_text: Theorem 1.5 establishes $\alpha \leq 5/2$, while the example of $K^+_{3,n-3}$ (which has Euler genus $\lceil\frac{n-5}{2}\rceil$) shows $\alpha \geq 1$, giving $1 \leq \alpha \leq 5/2$. The authors remark that the dependence on genus in Theorem 1.5 is likely not optimal.
rows.source_text: What is the smallest constant $\alpha$ such that every $Z_3$-flow-critical graph $G$ satisfies $|E(G)| \leq \frac{5}{2}|V(G)| + \alpha g(G) + O(1)$?
rows.defer_reason: 'What is the smallest constant alpha' — asks for an optimal value (with O(1) slack), not a single proposition.

rows.title: Belief on 4-vertex-critical arrangement graphs
rows.paper_title: Coloring circle arrangements: New $4$-chromatic planar graphs
rows.statement_text: We believe that the corona construction results in infinitely many 4-vertex-critical arrangement graphs.
rows.context_text: The paper's corona construction maps $\triangle$-saturated arrangements with a pentagonal face to arrangements with 4-chromatic 4-regular arrangement graphs, yielding an infinite family. The authors believe these are all vertex-critical, though this is not proved.
rows.source_text: We believe that the corona construction results in infinitely many 4-vertex-critical arrangement graphs.
rows.class_notes: Relies on the paper's corona construction and circle-arrangement graph definitions, none defined in the record.

rows.title: Conjecture on Sufficiency of Conditions E, R, T for Generic Tuples
rows.paper_title: Counting Dope Matrices
rows.statement_text: When $\Lambda$ is generic, Conditions E, R, and T are necessary and sufficient for an $m \times (n+1)$ matrix to be the multiplicity matrix of some polynomial $P$ with respect to $\Lambda$.
rows.context_text: Theorem 1 of the paper establishes that Conditions E, R, T are necessary and sufficient for a $2 \times (n+1)$ matrix to be a multiplicity matrix. The authors note that for $m > 2$ these three conditions are not sufficient in general (almost all matrices satisfying E, R, C for large $m = n$ are not multiplicity matrices), but conjecture sufficiency is restored when $\Lambda$ is generic. Further discussion is deferred to Section 8.
rows.source_text: When $\Lambda$ is generic, Conditions E, R, and T are necessary and sufficient for an $m \times (n+1)$ matrix to be the multiplicity matrix of some polynomial $P$ with respect to $\Lambda$.
rows.source_locator: arXiv:2205.09302 — Conjecture on Sufficiency of Conditions E, R, T for Generic Tuples
rows.status_semantics: Ankit Bisain (arXiv:2209.13811, September 2022; published BLMS 2024) resolves the conjecture by classifying dope matrices when the entries of Λ are algebraically independent (i.e., generic), establishing that Conditions E, R, T are necessary and sufficient for an m×(n+1) matrix to be the multiplicity matrix of a polynomial with respect to a generic tuple. The paper also provides asymptotic upper and lower bounds on the total number of m×(n+1) dope matrices.
rows.defer_reason: Multiplicity matrices of polynomials with respect to a tuple Lambda — polynomial algebra, not graph/hypergraph theory. Solved.

rows.title: Conjecture 1.3
rows.paper_title: Square roots of nearly planar graphs
rows.statement_text: The $\mathcal{H}$-square-root problem is NP-complete for the class $\mathcal{H}$ of planar graphs.
rows.context_text: The authors prove NP-completeness of the H-square-root problem for the class of 6-apex graphs (a proper minor-closed class), and note that 6-apex graphs lie at the bottom of the bounded-expansion hierarchy. They ask whether apex vertices are truly necessary or whether planarity alone already makes the problem hard, and state they believe the latter is the case.
rows.source_text: The $\mathcal{H}$-square-root problem is NP-complete for the class $\mathcal{H}$ of planar graphs.
rows.class_notes: NP-completeness of the planar-square-root recognition problem; precise but requires the complexity foundation.

rows.title: Informal conjecture on improving the $g(t)$ lower bound
rows.paper_title: Dense minors of graphs with independence number two
rows.statement_text: The factor $1/4$ in $g(t) \geq t(t+2)/8$ can likely be significantly improved. However it appears to be quite challenging, for example, to show that every graph with chromatic number at least $t$ contains a minor on $t$ vertices with at most one tenth of all possible edges missing.
rows.context_text: The authors define $g(t)$ as the maximum number of edges guaranteed in a $t$-vertex minor of any graph with chromatic number at least $t$. Mader's theorem yields $g(t) \geq t(t+2)/8$; the authors believe this is far from the true value, posing a density of $9/10$ as an example of a seemingly hard intermediate target for general graphs.
rows.source_text: The factor $1/4$ in $g(t) \geq t(t+2)/8$ can likely be significantly improved. However it appears to be quite challenging, for example, to show that every graph with chromatic number at least $t$ contains a minor on $t$ vertices with at most one tenth of all possible edges missing.
rows.source_locator: arXiv:2206.00186 — Informal conjecture on improving the $g(t)$ lower bound
rows.status_semantics: The conjecture that the factor $1/4$ in $g(t) \geq t(t+2)/8$ can be significantly improved has seen partial progress. Hendrey, Norin, Steiner, and Turcotte (arXiv:2307.01184, J. Graph Theory 2025) proved that graphs of average degree at least $t-1$ contain a $t$-vertex minor with at least $(\sqrt{2}-1-o(1))\binom{t}{2}$ edges — improving the density from $1/4$ to approximately $0.414$ — with an upper bound of $3/4+o(1)$. Since every graph with chromatic number $\geq t$ contains a $t$-critical subgraph of minimum degree $\geq t-1$, this result improves $g(t)$ accordingly. The conjecture's harder target of density $9/10$ (at most one tenth of edges missing) remains open.
rows.defer_reason: 'The factor 1/4 can likely be significantly improved' — improve-the-bound; the 9/10-density example is posed as an illustration of difficulty, not asserted as a conjecture.

rows.title: Conjecture 1.3
rows.paper_title: Sparse graphs with bounded induced cycle packing number have logarithmic treewidth
rows.statement_text: Maximum Independent Set is solvable in polynomial time in $\mathcal{O}_{k}$-free graphs.
rows.context_text: The paper proves that sparse $\mathcal{O}_k$-free graphs have logarithmic treewidth, making Maximum Independent Set polynomial in the sparse case (Corollary 1.2). A quasipolynomial algorithm is also given for general $\mathcal{O}_k$-free graphs, stopping just short of resolving this conjecture in full generality.
rows.source_text: Maximum Independent Set is solvable in polynomial time in $\mathcal{O}_{k}$-free graphs.
rows.defer_reason: computation-model layer out of scope for the X211-X229 waves: GTBase.complexity's cost-coupled prog/pcost core only supports positive 'there is a polynomial-time algorithm' claims, and the 2026-07-17 blocked-retargeting audit (meta/BLOCKED_RETARGETING_AUDIT.md) rejected 48/72 of the finite-witness encodings of poly-time / NP-hardness / dichotomy rows as unfaithful.
rows.class_notes: O_k-free = induced cycle packing number < k, adequately determined by title/context; poly-time MIS claim needs the computation model.

rows.title: Open Question: bounded twin-width for sparse $\mathcal{O}_k$-free graphs
rows.paper_title: Sparse graphs with bounded induced cycle packing number have logarithmic treewidth
rows.statement_text: Is there a function $f:\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ such that every $\mathcal{O}_{k}$-free graph that does not contain $K_{t,t}$ as a subgraph has twin-width at most $f(t,k)$?
rows.context_text: The paper shows that sparse $\mathcal{O}_k$-free graphs have logarithmic treewidth, but leaves open whether their twin-width is also bounded as a function of $t$ and $k$. The authors note that $\mathcal{O}_2$-free graphs without $K_{3,3}$ already yield a new family of counterexamples to bounded treewidth from forbidden induced subgraphs alone.

rows.title: Informal conjecture: MIS tractable in bounded-iocp graphs
rows.paper_title: Sparse graphs with bounded induced cycle packing number have logarithmic treewidth
rows.statement_text: Maximum Independent Set could be tractable in graphs with bounded $\mathrm{iocp}$ (induced odd cycle packing number).
rows.context_text: The paper establishes tractability of MIS for graphs with bounded induced cycle packing number ($\mathrm{icp}$, i.e., $\mathcal{O}_k$-free graphs) in the sparse case, and quasipolynomial time in general. The authors remark that extending this to bounded $\mathrm{iocp}$ would be a surprising and formidable generalisation of Conjecture 1.3 and of the known polynomial-time result for bounded $\mathrm{ocp}$ (odd cycle packing number).

rows.title: Open problem on happy triples for $l < k/2$
rows.paper_title: Improved bounds for the triangle case of Aharoni's rainbow generalization of the Caccetta-Häggkvist conjecture
rows.statement_text: It would be interesting to consider the best upper bound on the number of happy triples in a graph with $k$ edges and maximum degree at most $l$, for the regime when $l < k/2$.
rows.context_text: Lemma 2 establishes a tight bound on happy triples when $l \geq k/2$, achieved by specific extremal graphs. The authors note that their algorithmic/dynamic-programming approach gives little insight into the $l < k/2$ regime; for example, for $l=3$ and $k=3t$ the extremal graph output is $K_{t,3}$, which does not actually have maximum degree 3 for $t \geq 4$.
rows.source_text: It would be interesting to consider the best upper bound on the number of happy triples in a graph with $k$ edges and maximum degree at most $l$, for the regime when $l < k/2$.
rows.source_locator: arXiv:2206.10733 — Open problem on happy triples for $l < k/2$
rows.defer_reason: 'It would be interesting to consider the best upper bound' in the l < k/2 regime — asks for an unknown extremal value, not a proposition.

rows.title: Informal Conjecture on R(n;r,s) vs R'(n;r,s) near Turán density
rows.paper_title: Set-coloring Ramsey numbers via codes
rows.statement_text: We clearly have $R(n; r, s) \geq R'(n; r, s)$ and we believe that this estimate should be close to an equality when $s/r$ is close to the Turán density $1 - \frac{1}{n-1}$.
rows.context_text: The authors introduce the variant $R'(n;r,s)$, defined as the minimum $N$ such that every $(r,s)$-coloring of $K_N$ yields a color class with chromatic number at least $n$. They observe that $R(n;r,s) \geq R'(n;r,s)$ always holds, and that for the special case $s = r-1$ near-equality is confirmed by prior work of Alon et al. [1]. The informal belief is stated in Section 4 while studying the fixed-$n$ regime.
rows.source_text: We clearly have $R(n; r, s) \geq R'(n; r, s)$ and we believe that this estimate should be close to an equality when $s/r$ is close to the Turán density $1 - \frac{1}{n-1}$.
rows.source_locator: arXiv:2206.11371 — Informal Conjecture on R(n;r,s) vs R'(n;r,s) near Turán density
rows.status_semantics: The informal conjecture that R(n;r,s) ≈ R'(n;r,s) when s/r is near the Turán density 1−1/(n−1) has not been explicitly resolved, but the same group of authors published a follow-up (arXiv:2305.14132) that studies R(n;r,s) precisely in the intermediate range where s/r is close to 1−1/(n−1) by connecting it to the maximum size of error-correcting codes near the zero-rate threshold — the same coding-theoretic quantity that defines R'. This provides partial progress towards the belief, but a precise comparison R(n;r,s) ≈ R'(n;r,s) has not been confirmed in the verified literature.
rows.defer_reason: 'Should be close to an equality when s/r is close to the Turan density' — 'close to' is not quantified; no single proposition.

rows.title: Conjecture 6.2
rows.paper_title: Improved bounds for 1-independent percolation on $\mathbb{Z}^n$
rows.statement_text: For $p>0.55$, among models in $\mathcal{D}_{\geq p}(Q_{3})$ the signs model minimises the probability that $Q_{3}$ is connected.
rows.context_text: The signs model on $Q_3$ assigns each vertex independently '$+$' with probability $\theta$ and '$-$' otherwise, with an edge open iff both endpoints share the same sign (so each edge is open with probability $p=\theta^2+(1-\theta)^2$). Computational evidence strongly suggests this model minimises the connectivity probability of $Q_3$ for $p>0.55$; for smaller $p$ other models perform worse.
rows.source_text: For $p>0.55$, among models in $\mathcal{D}_{\geq p}(Q_{3})$ the signs model minimises the probability that $Q_{3}$ is connected.
rows.class_notes: Finite object (Q_3) but quantifies over all 1-independent measures with real edge probabilities >= p; 1-independence buildable, real-valued so rcfType idiom.

rows.title: Problem 6.4
rows.paper_title: Improved bounds for 1-independent percolation on $\mathbb{Z}^n$
rows.statement_text: What is the value of $p_{\mathrm{giant}}$?
rows.context_text: The paper establishes $p_{\mathrm{giant}}\leq 0.5847$ (when each edge of the hypercube $Q_n$ is open with probability at least $0.5847$ and $n$ is large, a giant component exists with high probability). The best lower bound remains $1/2$. Falgas-Ravry and Pfenninger conjectured $p_{\mathrm{giant}}=1/2$, but the exact value is unknown.
rows.source_text: What is the value of $p_{\mathrm{giant}}$?
rows.defer_reason: 'What is the value of p_giant?' — asks for an exact threshold value, not a proposition (the Falgas-Ravry–Pfenninger p_giant = 1/2 conjecture is a separate attributable statement).

rows.title: Conjecture 2
rows.paper_title: Coloring hypergraphs with excluded minors
rows.statement_text: For every integer $t\geq 2$ we have $h(t)=\left\lceil\frac{3}{2}(t-1)\right\rceil$. In other words, if a hypergraph $H$ does not contain $K_{t}$ as a minor, then $\chi(H)\leq\left\lceil\frac{3}{2}(t-1)\right\rceil$.
rows.context_text: The function $h(t)$ is the smallest integer such that every $K_t$-minor-free hypergraph is $h(t)$-colorable. The paper proves the lower bound $h(t)\geq\left\lceil\frac{3}{2}(t-1)\right\rceil$ by an explicit construction, and conjectures this lower bound is tight. The conjecture remains open even for $t=3$, where the best known upper bound is $4$.
rows.source_text: For every integer $t\geq 2$ we have $h(t)=\left\lceil\frac{3}{2}(t-1)\right\rceil$. In other words, if a hypergraph $H$ does not contain $K_{t}$ as a minor, then $\chi(H)\leq\left\lceil\frac{3}{2}(t-1)\right\rceil$.
rows.verification_note: Authored in X225.v:kt_minor_free_hypergraph_chromatic_three_halves_statement. Steiner Conjecture 2: h(t) = ceil(3(t-1)/2) for every t >= 2, rendered as the CONJUNCTION of the upper half (every loopless K_t-minor-free hypergraph is ceil_div (3 * t.-1) 2 - colourable, the open content and the source's own 'in other words' reading) and the tightness half (some loopless K_t-minor-free hypergraph is not colourable with one colour fewer, proved in the source). Vocabulary from the new shared foundation: [hg_loopless] (every hyperedge has >= 2 vertices), [hg_colourable E m] (no hyperedge monochromatic
rows.class_notes: RECOVERED from arXiv:2206.13635 (Steiner, 'Coloring hypergraphs with excluded minors'): hypergraphs are loopless (every hyperedge has size >= 2); W is independent if H[W] has no hyperedge and chi(H) is the least number of independent classes covering V(H). H_2 is a MINOR of H_1 if it is obtained by taking subhypergraphs and contracting hyperedges (identifying all vertices of a hyperedge); equivalently, an H_2-minor model is a family of disjoint connected branch sets (B_h) such that every hyperedge f of H_2 is witnessed by a hyperedge e of H_1 with e contained in the union of the B_h (h in f) and meeting each of them. Conjecture 2 (verbatim): 'For every integer t >= 2 we have h(t) = ceil(3(t-1)/2). In other words, if a hypergraph H does not contain K_t as a minor, then chi(H) <= ceil(3(t-1)/2).' The lower bound is proved in the paper, so the open half is the upper bound.

rows.title: Problem 1
rows.paper_title: Coloring hypergraphs with excluded minors
rows.statement_text: Is every $K_{3}$-minor-free hypergraph $3$-colorable?
rows.context_text: Conjecture 2 predicts $h(3)=3$, but the best known upper bound for the chromatic number of $K_3$-minor-free hypergraphs is $4$ (from Corollary 2 of the paper). Problem 1 isolates the smallest open case of Conjecture 2.
rows.source_text: Is every $K_{3}$-minor-free hypergraph $3$-colorable?
rows.verification_note: Authored in X225.v:k3_minor_free_hypergraph_three_colourable_statement. Steiner Problem 1 ('Is every K_3-minor-free hypergraph 3-colorable?'), stated in the affirmative per repository convention, on the same vocabulary as the companion row; [ceil_div (3 * 3.-1) 2] computes to 3, so implications_X225.v carries the corpus edge e049 as a Qed theorem (status=verified): the companion conjecture at t = 3 IS this problem.
rows.class_notes: RECOVERED from arXiv:2206.13635: same hypergraph-minor notion as axv_2206_13635_00 (K_3-minor = three disjoint connected branch sets pairwise joined by a hyperedge inside their union). Problem 1 (verbatim): 'Is every K_3-minor-free hypergraph 3-colorable?' -- the smallest open case (t = 3) of Conjecture 2, where the best known upper bound is 4.

rows.paper_title: Ramsey multiplicity and the Turán coloring
rows.statement_text: Every sufficiently large integer is polite.

rows.title: Conjecture 5.3
rows.paper_title: Ramsey multiplicity and the Turán coloring
rows.statement_text: There exist a mixed blowup coloring of $K_{r(k)-1}[2]$ for infinitely many $k$.
rows.context_text: The conjecture arises from Lemma 5.2, which reduces finding a mixed blowup coloring to exhibiting two Ramsey colorings of $K_{r(k)-1}$ that differ on a single vertex. The authors note they cannot establish this for any $k$, partly because $r(k)$ is only known for $k=3,4$, and for both values the Ramsey coloring of $K_{r(k)-1}$ is unique with all vertices having the same red and blue degree.
rows.source_text: There exist a mixed blowup coloring of $K_{r(k)-1}[2]$ for infinitely many $k$.
rows.class_notes: 'Mixed blowup coloring' is a paper-local notion not defined in the record; involves Ramsey numbers r(k) and 2-blowups, finite once recovered.

rows.title: Conjecture 5.4
rows.paper_title: Ramsey multiplicity and the Turán coloring
rows.statement_text: If $k\geq 4$ and $t$ is sufficiently large in terms of $k$, then any $(k,t)$-generalized lollipop is a two-color bonbon.
rows.context_text: Theorem 1.2 proves that adding $t\geq(1000kh)^{10}h^{10k}$ pendant edges to a $k$-critical graph $H_0$ with $h$ vertices yields a bonbon, but the proof requires $t$ at least exponentially large in $k$. Moreover, if $H_0=K_k$ then some lower bound on $t$ is necessary since adding $o(k^2/\log k)$ pendant edges to $K_k$ does not produce a bonbon. The conjecture proposes that sufficiently many pendant edges always suffice for any $k$-critical base graph.
rows.source_text: If $k\geq 4$ and $t$ is sufficiently large in terms of $k$, then any $(k,t)$-generalized lollipop is a two-color bonbon.
rows.class_notes: '(k,t)-generalized lollipop' and 'two-color bonbon' are paper-local; bonbon is an asymptotic Ramsey-multiplicity notion.

rows.title: Informal conjecture on the actual diameter
rows.paper_title: Small diameters and generators for arithmetic lattices in $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{R})$ and certain Ramanujan graphs
rows.statement_text: The bound (1.4) for the almost diameter is sharp and one may speculate whether the actual diameter is around the same length, i.e.\ $(2+o(1))\log 3V_\Gamma$.

rows.title: Informal Conjecture on Property (*) for d = o(n/log n)
rows.paper_title: On random irregular subgraphs
rows.statement_text: The irregular random subgraph $H = H(G)$ satisfies Property $(*)$ — that is, $m(H,k) = (1+o(1))n/(d+1)$ for all $0 \leq k \leq d$ — with high probability for all $d = o(n/\log n)$.

They also remark that for $d = \omega(n/\log n)$ the random subgraph model likely fails to satisfy Property $(*)$, and that new ideas would be required to establish Conjecture 1.2 in the full range.

rows.title: Problem 3
rows.paper_title: Perfect shuffling with fewer lazy transpositions
rows.statement_text: Does $U_t(n) = tn - \binom{t+1}{2}$?
rows.context_text: This generalises Problem 1 to the setting of shuffling $t$ distinguishable counters across $n$ positions using the fewest lazy transpositions. The upper bound $U_t(n)\leq tn-\binom{t+1}{2}$ is achieved by existing sweeping/divide-and-conquer constructions. When $t=n$ the problem reduces to Problem 1, which Theorem 2 answers negatively; the paper asks whether the trivial bound is tight for other values of $t$.
rows.source_text: Does $U_t(n) = tn - \binom{t+1}{2}$?
rows.status_semantics: Problem 3 asks whether U_t(n) = tn - C(t+1,2) holds for all t, where the upper bound is already established by sweeping/divide-and-conquer constructions and the t=n case is answered negatively by Theorem 2 of the source paper. A follow-up by Janzer, Johnson, and Leader (arXiv:2210.13286, October 2022) proves that U_2(n) = 2n-3, confirming the formula for t=2 and settling the corresponding conjecture of Groenland et al. Whether the formula holds for intermediate values of t remains open.
rows.defer_reason: Permutation / sorting-network statement, not a graph statement.

rows.title: Conjecture 2.1

rows.title: Conjecture (product structure with bounded tree-depth and tight clique size)
rows.paper_title: Product structure of graph classes with strongly sublinear separators
rows.statement_text: For any hereditary graph class $\mathcal{G}$ that admits $O(n^{1-\epsilon})$ separators, every $n$-vertex graph in $\mathcal{G}$ is a subgraph of the strong product of a graph $H$ with bounded tree-depth and a complete graph of size $O(n^{1-\epsilon})$.
rows.context_text: The abstract states that the paper investigates this conjecture. The proven results in the paper achieve the conclusion either with an extra $n^{\delta}$ factor in the clique size (for $H$ with constant tree-depth, any fixed $\delta\in(0,\epsilon)$) or with tree-depth $O(\log\log n)$ for $H$ when $\delta=0$; moreover, both limitations are shown to be best possible via isoperimetric inequalities for grid graphs. The conjecture in its strongest form — constant tree-depth of $H$ with clique size exactly $O(n^{1-\epsilon})$ — is investigated but not fully resolved.

rows.title: Question 6.1
rows.paper_title: List-avoiding orientations
rows.statement_text: Does every graph $G$ have a spanning subgraph with an Alon-Tarsi orientation in which each vertex $v$ has out-degree at least $\frac{1}{2}(\deg_{G}(v)-1)$?
rows.context_text: This question asks whether Conjecture 1.1 could be proved for every graph via the paper's Theorem 1.4 by finding a suitable Alon-Tarsi orientation, which would yield a stronger result. An affirmative answer would further imply that every graph $G$ on $n$ vertices and maximum degree $\Delta$ has a subgraph $H$ with at least $|E(G)|-n/2$ edges satisfying $\operatorname{AT}(H)\leq\lfloor\frac{1}{2}\Delta+\frac{3}{2}\rfloor$.

rows.title: Question 6.2
rows.paper_title: List-avoiding orientations
rows.statement_text: Does there exist a constant $C$ such that every graph $G$ of maximum degree $\Delta$ has a matching $M$ such that $\operatorname{AT}(G-M)\leq\frac{1}{2}\Delta+C$?
rows.context_text: This question is motivated by results showing that removing a matching from a graph can reduce upper bounds on coloring parameters such as the Alon-Tarsi number. It is noted that $C$ cannot be smaller than $\frac{1}{2}$, since for any odd $n$ and any maximum matching $M$ in $K_n$, $\operatorname{AT}(K_n-M)=\frac{n+1}{2}$. The authors ask specifically about matchings, inspired by Zhu's result on planar graphs and the result of Grytczuk and Zhu.

rows.title: Open question on twin-width over infinite fields
rows.paper_title: Twin-width V: linear minors, modular counting, and matrix multiplication
rows.statement_text: An intriguing question concerns the existence of such results over infinite fields (starting with $\mathbb{Q}$). We do not have a direct definition of twin-width of matrices over $\mathbb{Q}$ based on contraction sequences. However linear-minor freeness naturally carries to infinite fields, and thus, it is natural to consider that a class of matrices over $\mathbb{Q}$ has bounded twin-width if its closure under linear minors is not the set of all matrices.
rows.context_text: After establishing FPT matrix multiplication algorithms for matrices over finite fields $\mathbb{F}_q$ with bounded twin-width (Theorems 5–7), the authors raise the question of whether analogous results hold for matrices over infinite fields such as $\mathbb{Q}$. The text is truncated at this point, so the precise formulation of the question (likely involving the grid rank of a matrix) is not fully visible.

rows.status_semantics: The open problem asks for a sharp asymptotic for ex(G(n,p),P) when the minimum chromatic number of a graph not in P is 2 (i.e., P misses a bipartite graph), a case where the main theorem of the source paper yields only o(n^2). Clifton, Liu, Mattos, and Zheng (arXiv:2405.09486, 2024) directly answer the explicit sub-question posed by Alon–Krivelevich–Samotij: they prove that ex(G(n,p),P) = O(n^{2-epsilon}) with high probability for some epsilon=epsilon(P)>0, establishing a polynomial improvement over the trivial o(n^2) bound. For excluded complete bipartite graphs K_{s,t} they obtain the more precise bound O(n^{2-1/s}(log n)^{1/s}). However, determining the precise order of magnitude for general hereditary properties missing an arbitrary bipartite graph remains open.

rows.title: Conjecture 14
rows.paper_title: Graphs of Linear Growth have Bounded Treewidth
rows.statement_text: There exist functions $g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{N}$ and $h : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for any $c > 1$, every graph $G$ with growth $f_G(r) \leq cr$ is isomorphic to a subgraph of $T \boxtimes K_{g(c)}$ for some tree $T$ with growth $f_T(r) \leq h(c)r$.
rows.context_text: Theorem 13 shows that every graph $G$ with growth $f_G(r) \leq cr$ is a subgraph of $T \boxtimes K_{\lfloor 882c^3 \rfloor}$ for some tree $T$, but the tree $T$ itself may have exponential growth. Conjecture 14 proposes a rough characterisation of graphs of linear growth: if true, every subgraph $H$ of $T \boxtimes K_{g(c)}$ has growth $f_H(r) \leq g(c)h(c)r \in O(r)$, making the characterisation tight.
rows.source_text: There exist functions $g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{N}$ and $h : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for any $c > 1$, every graph $G$ with growth $f_G(r) \leq cr$ is isomorphic to a subgraph of $T \boxtimes K_{g(c)}$ for some tree $T$ with growth $f_T(r) \leq h(c)r$.
rows.class_notes: Growth function f_G(r) (ball sizes) is easy to define; statement is an existential-functions rough characterization of linear growth.

rows.title: Extension to H-free graphs
rows.paper_title: Turán graphs with bounded matching number
rows.statement_text: Determine the maximum possible number of edges of an $H$-free graph on $n$ vertices with matching number at most $s$, for general forbidden subgraphs $H$ (extending Theorem 1.1 beyond the case $H = K_{k+1}$).
rows.context_text: At the opening of Section 3, the authors note it may be interesting to extend Theorem 1.1 by replacing the forbidden clique $K_{k+1}$ by other forbidden subgraphs $H$. Proposition 3.1 settles this for color-critical $H$ when $s$ and $n$ are sufficiently large, but the problem for general $H$ (including non-color-critical graphs and small parameters) remains open.
rows.source_text: Determine the maximum possible number of edges of an $H$-free graph on $n$ vertices with matching number at most $s$, for general forbidden subgraphs $H$ (extending Theorem 1.1 beyond the case $H = K_{k+1}$).
rows.status_semantics: Gerbner (arXiv 2211.03272, J. Graph Theory 2024) directly took up this problem immediately after Alon–Frankl's paper, determining the maximum number of edges in n-vertex F-free graphs with matching number at most s apart from a constant additive term for all fixed F and s, with several exact results also obtained. The asymptotic form of the answer is thus settled for fixed parameters, but a complete exact determination for all H, n, s remains open. Ma and Hou (arXiv 2301.05625) subsequently extended the framework to the generalized Turán setting (counting copies of K_r).
rows.defer_reason: 'Determine the maximum possible number of edges' for general H is an open-ended determination request, not one proposition

rows.context_text: Theorem 1.6 establishes that admitting a homomorphism to a directed edge and having a cycle in the underlying undirected graph are both necessary conditions for the directed forcing property. rows.title: Conjecture 9.3
rows.paper_title: Random Embeddings of Graphs: The Expected Number of Faces in Most Graphs is Logarithmic
rows.statement_text: Let $G$ be a graph on $n$ vertices with minimum vertex degree $\Omega(n)$. Then $G$ satisfies $\mathbb{E}[F] = \Theta(\log(n))$.

rows.title: Conjecture 9.5
rows.paper_title: Random Embeddings of Graphs: The Expected Number of Faces in Most Graphs is Logarithmic
rows.statement_text: The expected number of faces in a non-orientable random embedding of the complete graph $K_{n}$ is at most $\ln(n) + O(1)$.
rows.context_text: The authors extend their investigation to non-orientable surfaces, where a random embedding is defined by choosing a random rotation system together with a random signature assigning each edge a sign independently with probability $1/2$. Computer simulations support a logarithmic behaviour analogous to the orientable case.

rows.title: Conjecture 9.6
rows.paper_title: Random Embeddings of Graphs: The Expected Number of Faces in Most Graphs is Logarithmic
rows.statement_text: Let $F^{-}$ be the random variable for the average number of faces in a non-orientable random embedding of some graph $G$. Then $\mathbb{E}[F^{-}] \leq \mathbb{E}[F]$.
rows.context_text: The authors conjecture that the expected face count in a non-orientable random embedding is always at most that of the orientable random embedding, for any graph $G$. The inequality is verified for toy models (including the dipole and chains of triangles joined by cut edges), and an analysis of Random Process A gives the bound $\mathbb{E}[F^{-}] \leq \frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}[F] + 1$ for the dipole.

rows.title: Informal Conjecture (second phase transition for all radii)
rows.paper_title: Shotgun assembly of random graphs
rows.statement_text: It seems likely that for every radius $r$ there should be a second phase transition around some threshold $t=t(n)$. By which we mean that, if $p=\omega(t(n))$, then $G$ is with high probability reconstructible from its $r$-neighbourhoods, while if $p=o(t(n))$ and $p=\omega(n^{-\frac{2r+1}{2r}})$, then with high probability $G$ is not reconstructible from its $r$-neighbourhoods.
rows.context_text: The paper establishes the existence of this second phase transition for all $r\geq 3$, but the question remains open for $r=1$ and $r=2$, for which only improved (but not matching) bounds are given.

rows.title: Question: finite families yielding clean H-free classes
rows.paper_title: Induced subgraphs and tree-decompositions VII. Basic obstructions in $H$-free graphs
rows.statement_text: For which finite families $\mathcal{H}$ of graphs is the class of all $\mathcal{H}$-free graphs clean?
rows.context_text: After proving Theorem 1.5 — which characterizes all single graphs $H$ for which the class $\mathcal{F}_H$ of $H$-free graphs is clean (precisely the subdivided star forests) — the authors pose the next natural step. They observe that any finite set $\mathcal{H}$ containing a subdivided star forest yields a clean class, but note that the converse fails (e.g., $\mathcal{H}=\{H, K_3\}$ for the unique double star on six vertices is also clean). A full description is deferred to a companion paper [6] by four of the five authors.
rows.source_text: For which finite families $\mathcal{H}$ of graphs is the class of all $\mathcal{H}$-free graphs clean?
rows.source_locator: arXiv:2212.02737 — Question: finite families yielding clean H-free classes
rows.status_semantics: The companion paper (arXiv:2311.05066, published in Advances in Combinatorics) by Alecu, Chudnovsky, Hajebi, and Spirkl proves Theorem 1.4: for a finite set $\mathcal{H}$ of graphs, the class of all $\mathcal{H}$-free graphs is clean if and only if there are only finitely many $n \in \mathbb{N}$ for which an $\mathcal{H}$-free $n$-array exists. This provides a complete necessary and sufficient condition in terms of $n$-arrays and reduces the question to understanding when $\mathcal{H}$-free arrays can be constructed for all large $n$. A direct structural characterization of exactly which families $\mathcal{H}$ satisfy this array condition — analogous to the single-graph case where $H$ must be a subdivided star forest — does not appear to follow immediately from these results.
rows.defer_reason: Characterization question ('for which finite families...'), not a single proposition.
rows.class_notes: 'Clean' is paper-local; full description deferred to a companion paper.

rows.title: Question 1.1
rows.paper_title: Graph-codes
rows.statement_text: Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a family of graphs closed under isomorphism. Is it true that $d_{\mathcal{H}}(n)$ tends to $0$ as $n$ tends to infinity if and only if $\mathcal{H}$ contains a graph with an even number of edges? Equivalently: is it true that for any fixed graph $H$ with an even number of edges, $d_H(n)$ tends to $0$ as $n$ tends to infinity?
rows.context_text: The authors define $d_H(n)$ as the maximum fraction of all graphs on $[n]$ forming an $H$-code (a family with no two members whose symmetric difference is a copy of $H$). If every member of $\mathcal{H}$ has an odd number of edges then $d_{\mathcal{H}}(n) \geq 1/2$, motivating the question of whether containing an even-edge graph is exactly the condition that forces $d_{\mathcal{H}}(n) \to 0$. The question is stated as the central open problem and noted in the concluding remarks to remain wide open.
rows.source_text: Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a family of graphs closed under isomorphism. Is it true that $d_{\mathcal{H}}(n)$ tends to $0$ as $n$ tends to infinity if and only if $\mathcal{H}$ contains a graph with an even number of edges? Equivalently: is it true that for any fixed graph $H$ with an even number of edges, $d_H(n)$ tends to $0$ as $n$ tends to infinity?
rows.status_semantics: The full Question 1.1 — whether $d_H(n)\to 0$ for every fixed graph $H$ with an even number of edges — remains open for general H-codes. Versteegen (arXiv:2310.19891, 2023) proved the analogous statement for the linear variant: if $H$ has an even number of edges then the density of a linear graph code avoiding $H$ is $O(2^{\binom{n}{2}}/\log n)$, and for almost all such $H$ it is at most $2^{\binom{n}{2}/n^{\varepsilon_H}}$ for some $\varepsilon_H>0$. This constitutes partial progress on Alon's question but does not settle it for non-linear codes.

rows.status_semantics: The question whether $d_{K_4}(n) = o(1)$ for general graph codes remains open as of May 2026. Versteegen (arXiv:2310.19891, 2023) made partial progress by proving that any linear graph code on $n$ vertices containing no copy of a graph $H$ with an even number of edges has size $O(2^{\binom{n}{2}}/\log n)$, which settles the analogue for linear codes; however, the general (non-linear) case of the question from Conjecture 1.1 / Question 1.1 of arXiv:2301.13305 is not resolved by this work. Several further papers cite arXiv:2301.13305 (including Gishboliner–Jin–Sudakov 2312.06610, Conlon–Lee–Versteegen 2404.17467, and Rancourt–Dodos–Tyros 2602.03298) but none were verified to resolve the full question.

rows.title: Open problem: tighter bounds for linear graph-codes
rows.paper_title: Graph-codes
rows.statement_text: Establish tighter bounds for the maximum possible cardinality of a linear family of graphs on $[n]$ in which no symmetric difference is a copy of a fixed graph $H$ with an even number of edges.
rows.context_text: The paper notes that for any fixed graph $H$ with an even number of edges the maximum size of a linear $H$-code is $o\bigl(2^{\binom{n}{2}}\bigr)$, but the proof via Ramsey's Theorem yields very weak quantitative bounds. Theorem 1.6 gives a tight result for the family $\mathcal{K}$ of all cliques as a model for what such tight results could look like.
rows.source_text: Establish tighter bounds for the maximum possible cardinality of a linear family of graphs on $[n]$ in which no symmetric difference is a copy of a fixed graph $H$ with an even number of edges.

rows.status_semantics: Versteegen (2023, arXiv:2310.19891) made significant progress on this problem: for any fixed graph H with an even number of edges, the maximum size of a linear H-code is O(2^{\binom{n}{2}} / \log n), and for almost all such H there exists \varepsilon_H > 0 giving the stronger bound 2^{\binom{n}{2}/n^{\varepsilon_H}}. These are substantially tighter than the original Ramsey-based bounds from the source paper. However, tight bounds matching a lower construction are not yet established in general, so the full problem remains open.

rows.title: Open problem: binary vectors with cube-length forbidden symmetric difference

The source paper proves it for stars, subdivided stars, and $P_t$ for $t \leq 5$. A subsequent paper in the Electronic Journal of Combinatorics (2025) extends $\eta$-boundedness to graphs without large induced matchings ($tK_2$-free), resolving a related conjecture from the source paper and adding another family of forests for which the conjecture holds. rows.title: Polynomial bounds for path-induced copy theorem (1.2)

rows.statement_text: Is there any hope for a comparable strengthening of 1.2, giving a polynomial bound on the chromatic number of graphs with no path-induced copy of a rooted tree $(T,r)$ and with clique number at most $t$?
rows.context_text: Scott, Seymour and Spirkl proved (Theorem 3.2) that excluding an induced tree and $K_{t,t}$ as a subgraph yields a polynomial bound $f(t)$ on average degree. The authors ask whether an analogous polynomial bound on chromatic number can be obtained for 1.2, which imposes the weaker hypothesis of bounded clique number at the cost of weakening the conclusion to a path-induced copy.

rows.statement_text: Are the profile and neighborhood complexities of $K_{t}$-minor-free graphs in $r^{\operatorname{\mathcal{O}}(t)}$?
rows.context_text: The second open problem asks whether the polynomial bound for proper minor-closed classes can be sharpened so that the degree of the polynomial grows only logarithmically (or polynomially) in the size $t$ of the excluded complete minor, rather than being a fixed polynomial independent of $t$.

rows.status_semantics: Beaudou, Bok, Foucaud, Quiroz, and Raymond (arXiv:2501.08895, 2025) prove that the r-profile complexity of $K_h$-minor-free graphs is in $O(h^{O(h)} \cdot r^{3h-3} \cdot k)$, improving Joret–Rambaud's earlier bound of $O_h(r^{h^2-1} k)$.
